fields.title: Gleanings Among the Sheaves
fields.subtitle: Short Readings for Heart and Soul
fields.description: A harvest of short readings gathered from Spurgeon’s sermons and writings — brief, vivid meditations on the Christian life. The original gleanings are gathered here under twenty themes, from the promises of God and the comfort of affliction to communion with Christ, the joy of salvation, and the hope of heaven — a page of Spurgeon for any moment or need.

fields.title: The Promises of God
fields.body_html:
The Preciousness of the Promises

To the believer, the promises of God are a mine of wealth that can never be exhausted. Happy is the one who knows how to trace their hidden veins and grow rich on their buried treasure. They are an armoury, holding every kind of weapon for attack and defence. Blessed is the one who has learned to enter that sacred arsenal, to put on the breastplate and the helmet, and to take up the spear and the sword. They are a surgery where the believer will find every kind of restorative and blessed medicine; there is an ointment for every wound, a tonic for every faintness, a remedy for every disease. Blessed is the one who is well trained in heavenly medicine and knows how to take hold of the healing power of God’s promises. The promises are a storehouse of food for the Christian. They are like the granaries Joseph built in Egypt, or the golden jar in which the manna was kept. Blessed is the one who can take the five barley loaves and fish of promise and break them until his five thousand needs are all supplied, and he can gather up baskets full of leftovers. The promises are the Christian’s Magna Carta of liberty; they are the title deeds of his heavenly estate. Happy is the one who knows how to read them well and call them all his own. Yes, they are the jewel room where the Christian’s crown jewels are kept. The regalia are his, to admire in secret today and to wear openly in Paradise later. He has already been given, as a king, the silver key that unlocks the strong room; even now he may grasp the sceptre, wear the crown, and put the imperial robe on his shoulders. Oh, how unspeakably rich are the promises of our faithful, covenant-keeping God! If we had the tongue of the greatest orator, and if that tongue were touched with a live coal from the altar, it still could not speak a tenth of the praise due to the exceedingly great and precious promises of God. No, even those who have entered into rest, whose tongues are tuned to the lofty, rapturous eloquence of cherubim and seraphim, can never tell the height and depth, the length and breadth, of the unsearchable riches of Christ that are stored in God’s treasure-house: the promises of His covenant of grace.

He Has Said

The apostles, like their Master, were always very ready with quotations. As inspired men they could always have used fresh words, yet they preferred (and in this they are an example to us) to quote old words that had long ago been stamped with the seal of divine authority: “He hath said.” Let us do the same. The words of ministers may be sweet, but the words of God are sweeter; and though original thoughts may have the charm of novelty, God’s ancient words have the ring, the weight and the value of old and precious coins, and they will never be found wanting on the day we need to use them. “He hath said” not only drives away doubts and fears; it also feeds all our graces. When the apostle wants to make us content, he says, “Be content with such things as ye have: for He hath said;” and when he wants to make us bold and courageous, he puts it forcefully like this: “He hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” So that we may boldly say, “The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.” When the apostle Paul wants to strengthen faith, he does it by feeding us from Scripture with the examples of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Gideon, Barak and Jephthah. When another apostle wants to calm us with a lesson in patience, he says, “Ye have heard of the patience of Job;” or if he wants to stir up our prayerfulness, he says, “Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed and prevailed.” “He hath said” is refreshing food for every grace and a decisive death-blow to every sin. Here you have nourishment for what is good and poison for what is evil. So search the Scriptures, because that is how you will grow healthy, strong and vigorous in the divine life.

But besides searching the promises by reading them and storing them in our memory, we should test them by experience. Each time a promise proves true, we should put a mark beside it and note that we too can say, as someone said long ago, “This is my comfort in my affliction; for Thy word hath quickened me.” “Wait on the Lord,” said Isaiah, and then he added, “Wait, I say, on the Lord,” as if his own experience led him to echo God’s voice to his hearers. Test the promise. Take God’s banknote to the counter and see whether it is cashed. Grasp the lever He provides to lift your trials and see whether it has real power. Throw this divine tree into the bitter waters of your Marah and learn how it sweetens them. Take this salt and throw it into the muddy waters, and see whether they are not made sweet, as the waters were long ago by the prophet Elisha. “Taste and see that the Lord is good ... for there is no want to them that fear Him.”

Inexhaustible Promises

God’s promises are not used up when they are fulfilled. Once kept, they stand just as good as before, and we may wait for them to be fulfilled a second time. Human promises, even at their best, are like a cistern that holds only a temporary supply; but God’s promises are like a fountain, never emptied and always overflowing. You may draw from them the whole measure of what they seem to contain, and they will still be as full as ever.

Obtaining Promises

Sometimes God gives His people fresh promises “by faith” just before a trial is about to come on them. It was so with Elijah. God said to him, “Go to the brook Cherith; behold, I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there.” This was at the beginning of the famine. He stayed there, and God kept the promise, for Elijah had obtained it by faith. Acting on faith and still depending on God, he stays at Cherith, and as a result of this faith God gives him a fresh promise: “Arise, get thee to Zarephath—I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee.” The faith that received the first promise won the honour of a second. So it is with us. If we have had a small promise and have seen it come true so far, if we have lived on it and made it the prop and support of our souls, surely God will give us another, greater one. And so, hurrying on from promise to promise, we will find that the promises are the rungs of the ladder Jacob saw, whose top reached to heaven. If you doubt and distrust the promise you have, you cannot expect God to reveal more to your soul. If you are afraid and unbelieving about the promise laid on your heart yesterday, you will not have a new one tomorrow. But act in simple faith on what God has already given you, and you will go from strength to strength, receiving grace upon grace and promise upon promise. The Spirit of God will whisper some promise into your soul that comes home with as much power as if an angel from heaven had spoken it to you, and you will “through faith” obtain promises that were out of your reach before.

Promises and Precepts

If you want the promises fulfilled for you, make sure you obey the command attached to the promise. Follow the example of Moses. Moses knew that a promise had been given to the people of Israel that they would be the world’s blessing; but to obtain it he had to practise self-denial, and so he “refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.” If the promise commands you to deny yourself, you cannot obtain it without doing so. Do it, and you will see it fulfilled. Or suppose the promise requires courage: use courage. Or does the promise require obedience? Be obedient. Remember how Rahab hung the scarlet cord from her window, because that was the test of her faith. Do the same. Whatever Christ has told you, do it. Neglect no command, however trivial it may seem. Do what your Master tells you without asking questions, for he is a poor servant who questions his Lord’s command. No doubt you too, like the Ethiopian official, will go on your way rejoicing once you have obeyed. Or is the promise made to those who bring back “a good report” of the land? Remember, Caleb and Joshua were the only two who obtained the promise, because they alone honoured God. So honour God yourself. Let a scoffing world hear your unchanging testimony that your God is good and true. Do not let your groaning and grumbling make people suspect that you have a hard master and that His servants have no joys, no comforts, no delights. Let it be known that the One you serve is no Egyptian slave-driver: His yoke is easy, His service a pleasure, His reward beyond words. “Them that honor Me, I will honor.” Be careful to obey the commands, and God will fulfil the promises for you.

fields.title: Faith and Assurance
fields.body_html:
Faith Necessary

“Whatsoever things are lovely, and pure, and of good report,” try to gain them; but remember that all these things put together, without faith, do not please God. Virtues without faith are whitewashed sins. Unbelief cancels everything. It is the fly in the ointment; it is the poison in the pot. Without faith, though you have all the virtues of purity, all the generosity of philanthropy, all the kindness of selfless sympathy, all the talents of genius, all the bravery of patriotism and all the firmness of principle, you have no claim to God’s acceptance, for “without faith it is impossible to please God.”

Faith nurtures every virtue; unbelief withers every virtue in the bud. Thousands of prayers have been stopped by unbelief. Many songs of praise that would have swelled the chorus of the skies have been smothered by unbelieving grumbling. Many a noble venture conceived in the heart has been blighted by unbelief before it could come to birth. Faith is the Christian’s Samson-lock: cut it off, and he can do nothing. While Peter had faith, he walked on the waves of the sea. But then a wave came behind him, and he said, “That will sweep me away;” and then another in front, and he cried out, “That will overwhelm me;” and he thought, “How could I be so presumptuous as to walk on top of these waves?” And as soon as he doubted, he began to sink. Faith was Peter’s lifebuoy; it kept him up. But unbelief sent him down. The Christian’s life could be described as always “walking on the water,” and every wave would swallow him up; but faith enables him to stand. The moment you stop believing, distress and failure follow. Oh, then, why do you doubt?

The Remedy for Doubts

The best way to have your faith strengthened is to have communion with Christ. If you commune with Christ you cannot be unbelieving. When His left hand is under my head and His right hand embraces me, I cannot doubt. When my Beloved sits at His table, and He brings me into His banqueting house, and His banner over me is Love, then I truly believe. When I feast with Him, my unbelief is ashamed and hides its head. Speak, you who have been led in the green pastures and made to lie down by the still waters; you who have seen His rod and His staff and hope to see them even when you walk through the valley of the shadow of death; speak, you who have sat at His feet with Mary, or laid your head on His chest with the well-loved John. Have you not found that when you have been near to Christ your faith has grown strong, and when you have been far from Him your faith has grown weak? It is impossible to look Christ in the face and then doubt Him. When you cannot see Him, you doubt Him; but you must believe when your Beloved speaks to you and says, “Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.” There is no hesitation then; you must rise from the lowlands of your doubt to the hills of assurance.

Increase of Faith

Most people have their faith increased through great trouble. We do not grow strong in faith on sunny days. It is in stormy weather that faith grows stronger. Faith is not something we achieve that drops like the gentle dew from heaven; it usually comes in the whirlwind and the storm. Look at the old oaks. How have they become so deeply rooted in the earth? Ask the March winds, and they will tell you. It was not the April showers or the sweet May sunshine that did it, but the rough wind shaking the tree back and forth, making its roots strike deeper and take a firmer hold. And so it must be with us. We cannot make great soldiers in the barracks at home; they must be made among flying bullets and thundering cannon. We cannot expect to make good sailors on the Serpentine; they must be trained far away on the deep sea, where the wild winds howl and the thunder rolls like drums in the march of the God of armies. Storms and gales are what make tough and hardy sailors. They see the works of the Lord, and His wonders in the deep. So it is with Christians. Great-faith must have great trials. Mr. Great-heart would never have been Mr. Great-heart if he had not once been Mr. Great-trouble. Valiant-for-truth would never have put those enemies to flight and been so valiant if the enemies had not attacked him first. We must expect great troubles before we will reach great faith.

The Author and Finisher of Faith

O Lord, how little the best of people are worth apart from You! How high they rise when You lift them up! How low they fall if You withdraw Your hand! In the middle of distress it is our joy when You enable us to say, “Though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him;” but if You take away Your Spirit, we cannot trust You even on the brightest day. When storms gather around us we can smile at them, if You are with us; but on the fairest morning that ever shone on a human heart, we doubt and fail if You are not still with us, to preserve and strengthen the faith You Yourself have given.

Faith and Feeling

We are saved by faith, not by feeling; yet holy faith and holy feeling are related as the root is to the flower. Faith is lasting, like the root that always stays buried in the soil; feeling comes and goes, and has its seasons. The bulb does not always send up its green stem, much less is it always crowned with its many flowers. Faith is the tree, the essential tree; our feelings are like the look of that tree in the different seasons of the year. Sometimes our soul is full of bloom and blossom, and the bees hum pleasantly and gather honey in our hearts. Then our feelings bear witness to the life of our faith, just as the buds of spring bear witness to the life of the tree. Later our feelings grow stronger still; and after we reach the summer of our delights, perhaps we begin to wither again into the dry yellow leaf of autumn. Sometimes the winter of our discouragement and despair will strip every leaf from the tree, and our poor faith stands like a blighted trunk without a trace of green. And yet, as long as the tree of faith is there, we are saved. Whether faith blossoms or not, whether it brings joyful fruit in our experience or not, as long as it is there and lasting, we are saved. Even so, we would have the most serious reason to distrust the life of our faith if it did not sometimes blossom with joy, and often bring forth fruit in holiness.

The Sin of Unbelief

Some think doubting God’s loving-kindness is a very small sin. In fact, some have even raised the doubts and fears of God’s people into fruits and graces and signs of great advance in experience. But to doubt the kindness, the faithfulness and the love of God is a very serious offence. A sin that makes God a liar can be no light sin; and yet unbelief in effect casts a foul and slanderous suspicion on the truthfulness of the Holy One of Israel. An offence that charges the Creator of heaven and earth with breaking His oath can be no small offence; and yet if I mistrust His oath and will not believe His promise, sealed with the blood of His own Son, I am treating God’s oath as unworthy of my trust, and so I really am accusing the King of Heaven of being false to His covenant and oath. Besides, unbelief toward God is the source of countless sins. As a black cloud is the source of many raindrops, so dark unbelief is the parent of many wrongs. It is a sin every believer should condemn and struggle against, should overcome if possible, and should certainly deeply repent of and hate.

Little-faith

One drawback of “little-faith” is that though it is always sure of heaven, it very seldom thinks so. Little-faith is just as secure of heaven as Great-faith. When Jesus Christ counts up His jewels on the last day, He will take the little pearls as well as the great ones. However small a diamond is, it is still precious because it is a diamond. So faith, however little, if it is true faith, is “like precious” with the faith the apostles received. Christ will never lose even the smallest jewel of His crown. Little-faith is always secure of heaven, because Little-faith’s name is in the book of eternal life. Little-faith was chosen by God before the foundation of the world. Little-faith was bought with the blood of Christ; yes, and he cost as much as Great-faith. “For every man a shekel” was the price of redemption. Every man, great or small, prince or peasant, had to redeem himself with a shekel. Christ has bought them all, little and great, with the same most precious blood. Little-faith is always secure of heaven, because God has begun the work in him and He will carry it on. God loves him, and He will love him to the end. God has provided a crown for him, and He will not let the crown hang there unused. He has built a mansion for him in heaven, and He will not let the mansion stand empty forever. Little-faith is always safe, but he very seldom knows it. If you meet him, he is sometimes afraid of hell, and very often afraid that God’s wrath rests on him. He will tell you that the country on the other side of the river can never belong to someone as low as he is. Sometimes it is because he feels so unworthy. Another time, he says, it is because the things of God are too good to be true, or he cannot believe they could be true for someone like him. Sometimes he is afraid he is not chosen; another time he fears he has not been called rightly, or has not come to Christ in the right way. Then his fear is that he will not hold on to the end, that he will not be able to persevere. Kill a thousand of his fears, and he is sure to have another army of them by tomorrow, for unbelief is one of those things you cannot destroy. You may kill it again and again, but it still lives. It is one of those wretched weeds that lie dormant in the soil even after it has been burned; it needs only a little encouragement or a little neglect, and it will sprout again. Now Great-faith is sure of heaven, and he knows it. He climbs to the top of Pisgah and looks out over the landscape. He tastes the sweetness of paradise even before he enters the pearly gates. He sees the streets paved with gold; he sees the walls of the city, whose foundations are precious stones; he hears the mysterious music of the glorified, and begins to smell the perfumes of heaven while still on earth. But poor Little-faith can hardly look at the sun. He very seldom sees the light. He gropes in the valley, and while everything is safe, he always thinks he is unsafe.

fields.title: In Sorrow and Affliction
fields.body_html:
Sorrow’s Discipline

The Lord gets his best soldiers out of the highlands of affliction.

The Privileges of Trial

It is said that when the stars cannot be seen by day from ordinary ground level, they become visible at once if you go down into a dark well. And it is certainly true that the Church usually sees the best of God’s promises in her darkest trials. As surely as God puts His children in the furnace, He will be in the furnace with them. I do not read that Jacob saw the angel until he was in a place where he had to wrestle; then the wrestling Jacob saw the wrestling angel. I do not know that Joshua ever saw the angel of God until he was near Jericho; then Joshua saw the angelic warrior. I do not know that Abraham ever saw the Lord until he had become a stranger and wanderer on the plains of Mamre; then the Lord appeared to him as a traveller. It is in our most desperate sorrows that we have our happiest experiences. You must go to Patmos to see the revelation. Only on the barren, storm-ringed rock, shut off from all the world’s light, can we find the right kind of darkness in which to see the light of heaven without being distracted by the shadows of earth.

Light in the Cloud

“The Lord turned the captivity of Job.” So our longest sorrows have an end, and there is a bottom to the deepest depths of our misery. Our winters will not frown forever; summer will soon smile. The tide will not go out forever; the floods must turn and come back. The night will not hang its darkness over our souls forever; the sun will still rise with healing in its wings. “The Lord turned the captivity of Job.” In the same way our sorrows will end when God has achieved His purpose in them. In Job’s case the purposes were these. First, that Satan might be defeated, beaten with his own weapons, his hopes blasted just when he had everything his own way. At Satan’s challenge God had stretched out His hand and touched Job in his bone and his flesh; and yet the tempter could not overcome him, but was rebuffed by those conquering words, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in Him.” When Satan is defeated, the battle will stop. The Lord also aimed to test Job’s faith. Many weights were hung on this palm tree, but it still grew straight. The fire had been fierce, yet none of the gold was lost; only the dross was burned away. Another purpose the Lord had was His own glory, and truly He was greatly glorified. Through the grace by which He held up His poor afflicted servant under the heaviest troubles that ever fell to anyone, God has won eternal renown for His great name and His wise counsels. God had another purpose, and that was served too. Job had been made holier by his afflictions. His spirit was mellowed, and any self-justification lurking inside him was thoroughly driven out. And now that God’s gracious purposes are met, He takes away the rod; He lifts the melted silver out of the glowing coals. God does not afflict willingly or grieve people for nothing, and He shows it by never afflicting them longer than necessary. He never leaves them a moment longer in the furnace than is absolutely needed to serve the purposes of His wisdom and love. “The Lord turned the captivity of Job.” So do not despair, afflicted believer. He who turned Job’s captivity can turn yours, like streams in the desert. He will make your vineyard blossom again and your field yield its fruit. You will again go out with those who celebrate, and once more the song of gladness will be on your lips. Do not let Despair fasten his cruel chains around your soul. Hope still, for there is hope in this matter. Keep trusting, for there is good reason for confidence. He will bring you up again, rejoicing, out of captivity, and you will yet sing His praise: “Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness.”

Clear Shining after Rain

Christ’s rule as King, as David describes it, is like “Clear shining after rain,” which makes the tender grass spring out of the earth. We have often seen it. After a heavy shower, or a long rainy spell, when the sun shines there is a delightful clearness and freshness in the air that we seldom notice at other times. Perhaps the brightest weather comes just when the rain has stopped, the wind has blown the clouds away, and the sun looks out from his rooms to gladden the earth with his smiles. So it is with the Christian’s tested heart. Sorrow does not last forever. After the pelting rain of adversity, again and again the clear shining comes. Tested believer, think about this. After all your afflictions there remains a rest for the people of God. A clear shining is coming to your soul when all this rain is over. When your time of rebuke has come and gone, it will be for you as it is for the earth when the storm has sobbed itself to sleep, the clouds have torn themselves to rags, and the sun looks out once more like a bridegroom in his glorious robes. To this end, sorrow works together with the joy that follows it, like rain and sunshine, to bring out the tender blade. Trouble and comfort work together for our good. “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ.” The clear shining after rain makes an atmosphere that refreshes plants and crops; and the joy of the Lord after seasons of sorrow makes the soul fruitful. This is how we grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

The Use of Trial

Trials teach us what we are. They dig up the soil and let us see what we are made of; they turn up some of the bad weeds to the surface.

Cross-Bearers

What an honour Simon of Cyrene had, to carry the cross for Jesus Christ! We could almost weep that we were not there, so that we might have had the honour of carrying Christ’s cross for Him. But we need not weep, because we will have His cross to carry if we are His people. There are no crown-wearers in heaven who were not cross-bearers here below. There will be no one in the crowd of the glorified who did not have their cross on earth. Do you have a cross, believer? Shoulder it bravely! Up with it! Go on your journey with steady steps and a rejoicing heart, knowing that since it is Christ’s cross it must be an honour to carry it, and that while you are carrying it you are in blessed company, for you are following Him.

The Christian’s Daily Cross

Believer, Christ Jesus gives you your crosses, and they are no poor gifts.

Consolation

Comfort is a gentle dew falling from heaven on dry hearts below; it is one of the choicest gifts of God’s mercy.

Sympathy

Sympathy is above all a Christian’s duty. Think about what a Christian is, and you will say that if everyone else were selfish, he should be unselfish; if there were no other heart anywhere with sympathy for the needy, there should be one in every Christian’s breast. The Christian is a “king”, and it is not fitting for a king to be meanly looking after himself. Was Alexander ever more royal than when his troops were suffering from thirst, and a soldier offered him a bowl full of the precious water, and he set it aside, saying it was not right for a king to drink while his subjects were thirsty; he would rather share their hardship with them? You whom God has made kings and princes, rule royally over your own selfishness, and act with the honourable generosity that suits the royal family of the universe. You are sent into the world to be saviours of others; but how can you be if you care only for yourselves? It is your calling to be lights; and does a light not burn itself up as it spreads its rays into the thick darkness? Is it not your duty and privilege to have it said of you, as of your Master, “He saved others, himself he cannot save?”

Comfort My People

God never gives His children a duty without giving them the means to carry it out; and when He tells us to “comfort” His people, we can be sure there are means by which they can be comforted. Child of God, are you at a loss for something to say to comfort an aching heart? Tell of the ancient things of former days. Whisper in the mourner’s ear about electing grace, redeeming mercy and Divine love. When you find someone troubled, tell them of the covenant, ordered well in all things. Tell them what the Lord did in former days, how He cut Rahab to pieces and wounded the dragon. Tell them the wonderful story of God’s dealings with His people. Tell them that God, who divided the Red Sea, can make a highway for His people through the deep waters of affliction; that He who appeared in the burning bush that was not consumed will hold them up in the furnace of trouble. Tell them of the marvellous things God has done for His chosen people: surely there is enough there to comfort them. Tell them that God watches the furnace as the goldsmith watches the refining pot. If that is not enough, tell them of their present mercies. Tell them that much is left, though much is gone. Tell them there is “now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus;” tell them that they are now accepted in the Beloved; tell them that they are now adopted and their standing is secure; tell them that Jesus is above, pleading their cause; tell them that though the pillars of the earth shake, God is a refuge for us; tell the mourner that the everlasting God does not fail or grow weary. But if this is not enough, tell them about the future. Whisper to them that there is a heaven with pearly gates and golden streets; tell them that

“A few more rolling suns at most, Will land him on fair Canaan’s coast,”

and so they can well bear their sorrows. Tell them that Christ is coming, that His sign is in the heavens, His coming is near, and He will soon appear to judge the earth with fairness and His people in righteousness. And if that is not enough, tell them all about the Saviour who lived and died. Take them to Calvary. Picture for them the bleeding hands and side and feet. Tell them of the thorn-crowned King of grief; tell them of the mighty Monarch of sorrow and blood, who wore the scarlet of mockery that was also the purple of the empire of grief; tell them that He Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree. In this way, with God’s blessing, you will carry out your mission and “comfort” one of His people. “Comfort ye My people, saith your God.”

The Refiner’s Fire

There is not a bar of silver in heaven’s treasury that has not been in the furnace on earth and been purified seven times. There is not a gem that the Divine Jeweller has not put through every kind of test. There is not a speck of gold in the Redeemer’s crown that has not been melted among the hottest coals to rid it of its impurities. This is true of every child of God. If you are a servant of the Lord, you must be tested “as gold is tried.”

Trouble Lightened

I am convinced that if we looked more to Jesus, our troubles would not seem so great or so painful. In the darkest night of trial, looking to Christ will clear the jet-black sky. When the darkness seems thick, like the darkness of Egypt, “darkness that might be felt,” even then a look to Jesus will be like a bright flash of lightning, just as vivid but not so brief. One glimpse of Him may well be enough for all our toil on the road. Looking to Him will light up the dreariest way. Cheered by His voice and strengthened by His power, we are ready to act and to suffer, as He did, to the end. Weary and troubled Christians, “look unto Him, and be lightened!”

Love in Chastening

God’s people are often disciplined, and the Lord’s hand lies heavy on them; yet there is a father’s goodness in their discipline and endless loving-kindness in their troubles. Have you ever heard this parable? A shepherd had a sheep that he wanted to lead into another, better field. He called it, and it would not come. He led it, and it would not follow. He drove it, but it would only go its own way. At last he thought to himself, “I will do this.” The sheep had a little lamb by its side, and the shepherd picked up the lamb in his arms and carried it away; and then the ewe came too. So it is with you. God has been calling you, and you did not come. Christ said, “Come,” and you would not. He sent affliction, and you would not come. At last He took your child away, and you came at once; you followed the Saviour then. You see it was loving work on the shepherd’s part. He only took the lamb to save the sheep, and the Saviour only took your child to heaven so that He might bring you there too. Oh, blessed afflictions, blessed losses, blessed deaths that end in spiritual life! You know that if someone wants to gather a harvest from a field, he first ploughs it. The field might complain and say, “Why these scars across my face? Why this rough turning over?” Because there can be no sowing until there has been ploughing; sharp ploughshares make furrows for good seed. Or take another picture from nature. A man wants to make a rusty piece of iron into a bright sword that will serve a great warrior. What does he do? He puts it in the fire and melts it. He takes away all its dross and removes all its tin. Then he shapes it with his hammer, beating it hard on the anvil. He tempers it in one fire after another until at last it comes out as a good blade that will not snap on the day of battle. This is what God is doing with you. I beg you, do not misread the book of God’s providence; for if you read it rightly it says: “I will have mercy on this man, and that is why I have struck him and wounded him. As many as I love I rebuke and chasten.” Come, then, let us return to the Lord, for He has wounded and He will heal; He has struck us and He will bind us up.

Enduring the Cross

“For the joy that was set before Him He endured the cross.” What was the joy? Oh, it is a thought that must melt a rock and move a heart of iron: the joy set before Jesus was mainly the joy of saving us. I know it was the joy of doing His Father’s will, of sitting down on His Father’s throne, of being made perfect through suffering; but still I know that the grand, great motive for the Saviour’s enduring the cross was the joy of saving us. Do you know the joy of doing good to others? If you do not, I pity you, because of all the joys God has left in this poor wilderness, this is one of the sweetest. Do you know it? Have you never felt that divine joy when your gold has been given to the poor and your silver dedicated to the Lord, when you gave it to the hungry, and then went off by yourself and said, “I feel it is a joy worth living for, to feed the hungry and clothe the naked and do good to my poor suffering fellow human beings”? This is the joy Christ felt. It was the joy of feeding us with the bread of heaven; the joy of clothing poor naked sinners in His own righteousness; the joy of finding a home for homeless souls, of rescuing us from the prison of hell and giving us the eternal joys of heaven. See how great His love was, that led Him to endure the cross and despise the shame so that He might save sinners. Truly Christ’s love “passeth knowledge!” Christians, if Christ endured all this for the joy of saving you, will you be ashamed of bearing or suffering anything for Christ? Surely love for Him who has loved us so much should make us willing to endure anything for His sake. Do you feel that following Christ will cost you, that you will lose honour, position, wealth? Do you feel that being a Christian brings ridicule and reproach on you? And will you turn aside because of these little things, when He would not turn aside but endured the cross and despised the shame? No; by the grace of God let every Christian say,—

“Now for the love I bear His name, What was my gain I count my loss; My former pride I call my shame, And nail my glory to His cross.”

“For me to live is Christ; to die is gain.” Living, I will be His; dying, I will be His. I will live for His honour and serve Him wholly. I will take up my cross and follow Him, rejoicing if I am counted worthy to suffer for His name’s sake.

Sweetness in Sorrow

Looking back on times of affliction, do you not feel that, in spite of the trials, they were times when you had unusual peace and happiness in your heart? There is a sweet joy that comes to us through sorrow. The bitter wine of sorrow acts as a tonic on the whole system. The sweet cup of prosperity often leaves a bitter taste; but the bitter cup of affliction, when it is made holy, always leaves a sweet flavour in the mouth. There is joy in sorrow. There is music in this harp, though its strings are all loosened and broken. There are a few notes from this mournful lute that we never hear from the loud trumpet. We get a softness and melody from the cry of sorrow that we never get from the song of joy. Must we not explain this by the fact that in our troubles we live nearer to God? Our joy is like a wave dashing on the shore; it throws us onto the earth. But our sorrows are like the wave going back out, which draws us again into the great depth of God. We would have been stranded high and dry on the shore if it had not been for that receding wave, that ebbing of our prosperity, which carried us back to our Father and our God. Blessed affliction! It has brought us to the mercy seat, given life to prayer, kindled love, strengthened faith, brought Christ into the furnace with us, and then brought us out of the furnace to live with Christ more joyfully than before.

fields.title: The Christian Warfare
fields.body_html:
The Joy of Victory

The Christian’s battlefield is here, but the victory parade is above. This is the land of the sword and the spear; that is the land of the wreath and the crown. This is the land of the garment rolled in blood and the dust of the fight; that is the land of the trumpet’s joyful sound, the place of the white robe and the shout of conquest. Oh, what a thrill of joy all the blessed will feel when their conquests are complete in heaven; when death itself, the last enemy, is slain; when Satan is dragged captive behind Christ’s chariot wheels; when the great shout of universal victory rises from the hearts of all the redeemed! What a moment of pleasure that will be!

We know something of the joy of victory even here. Have you ever struggled against an evil heart and at last overcome it? Have you ever wrestled hard with a strong temptation and known what it is to sing with thankfulness, “When I said my feet slipped, Thy mercy, O Lord, held me up?” Have you, like Bunyan’s Christian, fought Apollyon and, after a fierce contest, put him to flight? Then you have had a foretaste of the heavenly triumph, just a glimpse of what the final victory will be. God gives you these partial victories as down payments on the future. Go on and conquer, and let each conquest, though harder and more fiercely fought, be a pledge to you of the victory of heaven.

Safety in Conflict

The way God keeps His people safe is not by keeping their enemies from attacking them, but by holding them up while they are in the fight. It is no great thing to keep yourself safe behind a wall that cannot be climbed. But to stand where arrows fly thick as hail, where lances are thrust with fury, where sword-strokes fall on every side, and in the middle of it all to prove unwoundable, unconquerable, deathless: that is to bear a divine life no human power can defeat. Such is the Christian’s calling. God will put us where we must be tested and tempted. If we are not tested, there is no honour to Him who keeps us; and if we are not tempted, there is no gratitude to His grace for rescuing us from temptation. The Lord does not put His plants in a hothouse, as some gardeners do. No, He sets them out in the open air, and if frost is coming He says, “Ah, but no frost can kill them, and they will be all the sturdier in summer for the cold of winter.” He does not shelter them from the heat of the sun or the chill of the night. In this world we must have trouble, and plenty of it, because it is through much tribulation that we inherit the kingdom. What God does for His people is this: He keeps them in trouble, preserves them in temptation, and brings them out of all their trials with joy. So, Christian, you may rejoice in your security; but you must not think you will not be attacked. You are like a stream from Lebanon, to be dashed down many a waterfall, broken over many a rough rock, blocked by many a huge stone, hindered by many a fallen tree; but you are to rush forward with the irresistible force of God, sweeping everything away, until at last you find the place of your perfect rest.

War against Sin

Christian, never take hold of sin except with a gauntlet on your hand. Never go to it in the kid glove of friendship. Never speak of it delicately, but always hate it in every shape. If it comes to you as a little fox, watch out, for it will spoil the grapes. Whether it leaps toward you as a roaring lion looking for someone to devour, or approaches in an attractive form with graceful manners, trying to lure you into sin with pretended affection, beware: its hug is death and its embrace is destruction. You are to make war on sin of every kind, of the lips, of the hand, of the heart. However gilded with profit, however varnished with the respectability of morality, however praised by the great or popular with the crowd, you are to hate sin everywhere, in all its disguises, at every time and in every place. Not one sin is to be spared. Against all of it a complete and total war of extermination is to be declared.

Endure Hardness

Soldier of Christ, you will have hard fighting to do. There is no feather bed for you; there is no riding to heaven in a carriage. The rough road must be walked, mountains climbed, rivers forded, dragons fought, giants slain, difficulties overcome and great trials borne. It is not a smooth road to heaven; those who have gone only a few steps along it have found it rough and rugged. Yet it is pleasant; it is the most delightful journey in the whole world. That is not because it is easy in itself. It is pleasant only because of the company, because of the sweet promises we lean on, because of our Beloved who walks with us through all the rough and thorny thickets of this vast wilderness. Christian soldiers, expect conflict: “Think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you.” As surely as you are a child of God, your Saviour has left you this as His legacy: “In the world ye shall have tribulation.” Yet remember that this “tribulation” is the way to “enter the kingdom;” so “endure hardness as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”

The Fight of Faith

Like the Spartans, every Christian is born a warrior. It is his destiny to be attacked; it is his duty to attack. Part of his life will be taken up with defending. He will have to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints; he will have to resist the devil and stand against all his schemes; and having done everything, still stand. Yet he will be a poor Christian if he only defends; he must be someone who goes out against his enemies. He must be able to say with David, “I come against thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel whom thou hast defied.” He must wrestle not with flesh and blood but against principalities and powers. He must have weapons for his warfare, not worldly ones, but “mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds.” He must not be content to live in the well-guarded fortress; he must go out to attack the enemy’s castles and drive the Canaanites out of the land. But there are many ways in which a Christian may largely forget that he is a soldier. And sadly, there are quite a few who, if they are Christians at all, certainly know very little of the daily warfare the Captain of our salvation calls His disciples to. They have a soft religion, a religion that avoids opposition, a reed-like religion that bends before every gust. It is unlike the cedar of godliness that stands tall in the middle of the storm and claps its branches in the hurricane for sheer joy of triumph, though the whole earth is in arms around it. Such people lack the faith that shares in the glory. Though they are saved, their names will not be found among the mighty men who, for our Great Commander’s sake, are willing to lose everything and go outside the camp bearing His reproach. Oh, let us never be content with such inglorious ease, but fight the Lord’s battles earnestly and bravely. Is it a small thing for a follower of Christ to lose the immortal honour of serving the Lord? What will people not do to win fame? And when that honour lies at our very door, shall we lazily turn aside and throw our glory on the ground? Let us get up and get to work, for it is no light thing to lose the honour of being a faithful servant of Christ.

Steadfastness

If you had more faith, you would be as happy in the furnace as on the mountain of delight. You would be as glad in famine as in plenty. You would rejoice in the Lord when the olive gave no oil, as well as when the vat was bursting and overflowing. If you had more confidence in God, you would be tossed up and down far less; and if you were nearer to Christ, you would waver less. At times you can defy Satan’s rage, boldly meet every attack and resist every temptation; but too often you are fearful and undecided, ready to run from the fight instead of resisting bravely. But if you always remember Him who endured such hostility from sinners against Himself, you could always be firm and steadfast. Live near your Master, and you will not be so changeable and unsure. Beware of being like a weathervane. Ask God that His law may be written on your heart as if in stone, not as if in sand. Ask that His grace may come to you like a river, not like a brook that dries up. Ask that you may keep your conduct always holy, and that your path may be like the shining light that does not pause but burns brighter and brighter until the full day. Ask that the “God of all grace may establish, strengthen, settle you.”

The Triumphant Deliverance

When the Israelites left the land of Egypt, they took all their possessions with them, according to the word of the Lord: “Not a hoof shall be left behind.” What does this teach us? Not only that all God’s people will be saved, but that everything God’s people ever had will be restored. Everything Jacob ever took down to Egypt will be brought out again. Did I lose a perfect righteousness in Adam? I will have a perfect righteousness in Christ. Did I lose happiness on earth in Adam? God will give me much happiness here below in Christ. Did I lose heaven in Adam? I will have heaven in Christ. For Christ came not only to seek and save the people who were lost, but that which was lost: the whole inheritance as well as the people, all their property. Not just the sheep, but the good pasture the sheep had lost; not only the prodigal son, but all the prodigal son’s estates. Everything was brought out of Egypt; not even Joseph’s bones were left behind. The Egyptians could not say they had a scrap of the Israelites’ property, not even one of their kneading troughs or one of their old garments. And when Christ has brought everything under Himself, the Christian will not have lost a single atom through the hardships of Egypt, but will be able to say, “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” O hell, where is your triumph? You have not one flag or pennant to show for your victory; there is not a helmet left on the battlefield; there is not one trophy you can set up in hell to mock Christ. He has not only rescued His people; they have gone out with flags flying. Stand and wonder, and love the Lord who rescues all His people like this. “Great are Thy works, O Lord, and marvellous are Thy doings; and that my soul knoweth right well.”

More than Conquerors

The Christian is to be a conqueror at last. Do you think we are to be the drudges and slaves of sin forever, sighing for freedom and never able to escape its bondage? No! Soon the chains that hold me will be broken, my prison doors will be opened, and I will rise to the glorious city, the home of holiness, where I will be completely free from sin. We who love the Lord are not to live in Meshech forever. The dust may soil our robes now, but the day is coming when we will rise, shake ourselves free of the dust and put on our beautiful garments. It is true that we are now like Israel in Canaan. Canaan is full of enemies; but the Canaanites will and must be driven out, and the whole land from Dan to Beersheba will be the Lord’s. Christians, rejoice! You will soon be perfect, soon free from sin, without one wrong inclination or one evil desire. You will soon be as pure as the angels of light; more than that, wearing your Master’s garments, you will be “holy as the holy One.” Can you take that in? Is it not the very sum of heaven, the rapture of bliss, the song of the hilltops of glory, that you will be perfect? No temptation can reach you, and if it could, it would not harm you, because there will be nothing in you that could in any way feed sin. It would be like a spark falling on the ocean; your holiness would put it out in a moment. Yes, washed in the blood of Jesus, you will soon walk the golden streets, white-robed and white-hearted too. Oh, rejoice in the prospect so close at hand, and let it strengthen you for the present fight.

The Christian Warfare

The Christian is called to fight a tough battle. It is not one that show-soldiers could win, no easy skirmish to be won by someone who rode into battle on a sunny day, looked at the enemy army, turned his horse around and daintily dismounted at the door of his silk tent. It is not a campaign to be won by someone who is a raw recruit today and foolishly imagines that one week of service will guarantee a crown of glory. It is a lifelong war; a contest that will take all our strength if we are to win; a battle that might make the stoutest heart tremble; a fight the bravest would shrink from, if he did not remember that the Lord is on his side. So whom shall he fear? God is the strength of his life: of whom shall he be afraid? This fight is not one of brute force or physical might; if it were, we might win it sooner. It is all the more dangerous because it is a struggle of the mind, a contest of the heart, a wrestling of the spirit, and often an agony of the soul.

Are you surprised that the Christian is called to conflict? God never gives strong faith without a fiery trial. He will not build a strong ship without putting it through very mighty storms. He will not make you a mighty warrior if He does not mean to test your skill in battle. The sword of the Lord must be used. The blades of heaven must be struck against the armour of the evil one; and yet they will not break, because they are made of true Jerusalem metal, which will never snap. We will conquer if we begin the battle in the right way. If we have sharpened our swords on the cross, we have nothing at all to fear. Though we may sometimes be knocked down and thrown into confusion, we will certainly put all our enemies to flight in the end, for we are the sons of God even now. Why then should we be afraid? Who will tell us to “stay” if God tells us to advance?

fields.title: Strength in Weakness
fields.body_html:
Strength Through Weakness

The way to grow strong in Christ is to become weak in yourself. God pours no power into a person’s heart until that person’s own power has all been poured out. The Christian’s life is one of daily dependence on the grace and strength of God.

The Secret of Strength

Are you proud, believer, because you have been useful to the Church and done some small service in your time? Who makes you different from anyone else, and what do you have that you did not receive? Have you shed a little light on the darkness? Ah, but who lit your candle, and who keeps you shining and stops you from going out? Have you overcome temptation? Do not hang up your banner or decorate your own chest with the glory; for who made you strong in the battle? Who sharpened your sword and gave your arm the nerve to strike the enemy? Remember, you have done nothing at all by yourself. If today you are a vessel for honour, decorated and gilded, if you are now a precious vase filled with the sweetest perfume, you did not make yourself so. You are the clay, but who is the potter? If you are a vessel for honour, you are still not a vessel for your own honour, but for the honour of the One who made you. If you stand among your fellow human beings as the angels stand above the fallen spirits, chosen and set apart from them, remember that it was no goodness in you that got you chosen. Nor was it any effort or power of your own that lifted you out of the miry clay, set your feet on the rock and made your steps secure. Take the crown off your proud head and lay your honours at the feet of the One who gave them to you. Cover your face with the cherubim and seraphim, and cry, “Not unto us, not unto us, but unto His name be all the glory forever and ever.”

And when you are bowed down in humility like this, be ready to learn another lesson: never depend on yourself again. If you have anything to do, do not go out to do it leaning on human strength. First bend your knee and ask for power from the One who makes you strong, and then you will come back from your work rejoicing. But if you go in your own strength, you will break your ploughshare on the rock. You will sow your seed beside the salt sea on the barren sand, and in years to come you will look at the bare fields, and they will not give you so much as a single blade of grain to gladden your heart. “Trust ye in the Lord forever: for in the Lord Jehovah is everlasting strength.” That strength is not available to you as long as you rest on any strength of your own. He will help you if you confess your weakness; but if you are strong in yourself, He will take His own power away from you, and you will stumble and fall. So learn the grace of depending on God every day, and in that way you will be clothed with fitting humility.

Increase of Strength

The troubles that attack the plants of God’s planting while they are saplings are very small compared with the storms that blow around them once they have become strongly rooted, like cedars. As surely as our strength increases, our sufferings, trials, labours or temptations will multiply. God never gives anyone His power to be stored away. The food He gives to strengthen us, like the manna the Israelites gathered in the wilderness, is meant to be used right away. When the Lord puts on our feet the iron shoes He has promised us in the covenant, it is so that we may walk in them, not so that we may put them in our museum and gaze at them as curiosities. If He gives us a strong hand, it is because we have a strong enemy to fight. If He gives us a great meal, as He did Elijah long ago, it is so that we may go on a forty-day journey in the strength of that meal.

fields.title: Communion with Christ
fields.body_html:
The Soul Satisfied in Christ

Whoever delights in having the Lord Jesus has everything the heart could wish for. As for created things, they are like shallow, deceptive brooks; they fail to meet our needs, let alone our wishes. “The bed” of earthly enjoyment “is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it, and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it;” but in Jesus there is room for the imagination’s furthest stretch and widest range. When Jesus is enjoyed, He fills all our other mercies with fullness. His house is full when He is there; His throne of grace is full when He sits on it; His guest room is full when He is master of the feast. “The creature without Christ is an empty thing, a lamp without oil, a bone without marrow;” but when Christ is present, our cup overflows and we eat bread to the full. A meal of vegetables, when we have communion with Him, is as rich a feast as a fattened ox, and our narrow cottage is as fine a mansion as the great house of the rich. Do not go wandering, you hungry wishes of my soul; stay at home and feast on Jesus. If you go wandering you will starve, because every other love is empty and not worth wanting. Stay with Christ, eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.

Memorials of Jesus

The Church’s love goes beyond the person of the Bridegroom and reaches everything connected with Him. “All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad.” Even His clothes are precious to her. She rejoices to sing of Him in His priestly garments.

“The mitred crown, the embroidered vest, With graceful dignity He wears; And in full splendor on His breast The sacred oracle appears.”

Dressed in His royal robes, He is no less glorious in her eyes; she loves to see His crown and acknowledge her King. There is not a word His lips have spoken, nor a place His foot has trodden, nor a vessel His hands have touched, that is not wholly sacred to her. We do not worship the ragged relics Rome hoards so fondly; but we have other and far better memorials, holy things of priceless worth. His written Word, over which we can almost still see that loving hand moving as it did when, many years ago, it wrote each letter; the echo of His voice, gone but not yet buried in silence; His cup of wine not yet empty; His blood still flowing, and His blessing still breathing peace on us: all these still remain, and are valued above any price. We value His ordinances, and we glory in His teaching, however much the worldly-wise may despise it. His service is our delight; to stand at His gates is an honour, and to run ahead of His chariot is bliss. As for His people, we greet them as saints, we call them our brothers and sisters, and they are very near and dear to us for His sake. The poorest beggar in His Church means more to us than the proudest king outside it. “Because he belongs to Christ” is always reason enough for our love to flow out, for everything that is His is dear to us.

The Fulness of Christ

Even at our very best, we know nothing of much of the matchless sweetness of Christ. We will never exhaust His goodness with our praise, for He is always so fresh, and has so much of the dew of His youth, that every day there is a new song to sing. We will find Him a new Christ every day of our lives, and yet He is always the same; His surpassing excellence and inexhaustible fullness keep renewing our love. O Jesus, no one can guess how great the least of Your attributes is, or how rich the poorest of Your gifts.

Thoughts of Christ

Jesus! What endless sweetness there is in His name! Our impressions as we look at Him are like some of those crystals you have seen. Hold one up one way and you see one light; turn it another way and you see another; whichever way you turn it, you always see some precious sparkle of light and some new colours springing into view. Take Jesus as your theme. Consider Him. Think about His relationship to your own soul, and you will never come to the end of that one subject. Think of His eternal relationship to you, and also of your known and evident relationship to Him since you were called by His grace. Think how He has become your brother; how His heart has beaten in sympathy with yours; how He has kissed you with the kisses of His love, and His love has been sweeter to you than wine. Look back on some happy, sunny places in your story where Jesus has whispered, “I am yours,” and you have said, “My beloved is mine.” Think of some special moments when an angel seemed to stoop from heaven, take you on his wings and carry you up to sit in the heavenly places where Jesus sits, so that you might commune with Him. Or think of moments when you have had what Paul valued so highly, fellowship with Christ in His sufferings; when you have felt you could die for Christ, just as in the rich experience of your baptism you died with Him and rose with Him. Think of your relationship to Christ that is still to unfold in heaven. Imagine that the hour has come when you will “greet the blood-besprinkled hand on the eternal shore,” and the Lord Jesus will greet you as “more than a conqueror” and put on your head a crown brighter than the stars. Oh, take Jesus as your constant theme, and every day you will find fresh thoughts rising out of His grace, His beauty and His glory. In Him you have an unfailing source of delight, an object of attraction and a centre for your love.

Communion with Christ

One hour with Christ is worth an eternity of all the joys of earth; and communion with Him is the best, the surest and the most thrilling foretaste of the bliss of heaven.

fields.title: The Love of Christ
fields.body_html:
The Knowledge of Christ’s Love

Knowing the love of Christ is the mark that sets God’s people apart. Without exception, everyone who has passed from death to life has learned this, whatever else they may not know. And without exception, everyone who is not saved knows nothing of it, whatever else they may know. For to know the love of Christ, to taste its sweetness, to grasp it personally, by experience and with life in it, as it is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, is the privilege of God’s child alone. This is the secure enclosure the stranger cannot enter. This is the Lord’s garden, so well protected by walls and hedges that no wild boar from the woods can get in. Only the redeemed of the Lord will walk here. They, and only they, may pick its fruits and enjoy its delights.

How important, then, is the question: Do I know the love of Christ? Have I felt it? Do I understand it? Is it poured out in my heart? Do I know that Jesus loves me? Is my heart brought to life, stirred, warmed and drawn toward Him by the great truth it recognizes and rejoices in, that Christ has really loved me, chosen me and set His heart on me?

But while it is true that every child of God knows the love of Christ, it is just as true that not all God’s children know this love to the same degree.

In Christ’s family there are babies, young men, strong men and fathers. And just as they grow and make progress in everything else, they certainly make progress here. In fact, growth in love, a fuller grasp of Christ’s love, is one of the best and surest measures for testing whether we have grown in grace. If we have grown in grace, it is absolutely certain that we will have advanced in knowing the love of Christ and returning it. Many have believed in Jesus and know a little of His love; but, oh, how little they know compared with others who have been brought into the inner room and given the spiced wine of Christ’s pomegranate to drink. Some have begun to climb the mountain, and the view at their feet is lovely and very fair; but it is not the landscape that would greet their eyes if they could only stand where mature saints stand, and look east and west, north and south, and see all the lengths and breadths and depths and heights of the love of Christ, which passes knowledge.

Christ Altogether Lovely

In calling the Lord Jesus “altogether lovely,” the Church declares that she sees nothing in Him that she does not admire. The world may rail at His cross and call it shameful; to her it is the very centre and soul of glory. A proud and scornful nation might reject their King because of His manger cradle and peasant clothes, but in her eyes the Prince is glorious in this poor clothing. He is never without beauty to her; His face is never marred to her, nor His glory stained. She presses His pierced feet to her heart and looks on their wounds as jewels. Fools stand by His cross and find plenty to joke and sneer about; she finds nothing but solemn reason for reverent worship and boundless love. Looking at Him in every office, position and relationship, she cannot find a flaw; in fact, the very thought of imperfection is driven far away. She knows His perfect Godhead and His spotless humanity too well to give a moment’s shelter to the idea of a blemish in His flawless person. She detests every teaching that lowers Him. She rejects the most splendid drapery that would hide His beautiful features. She is so jealous for His honour that she will listen to no spirit that does not bear witness to His praise. A hint against His pure conception or His unstained purity would stir her soul to holy anger; she would be quick to denounce the heresy and relentless in putting it to death. Nothing has ever roused the Church’s anger so fully as a word against her Head. To all true believers this is high treason, an offence that cannot be treated lightly. Jesus is without a single spot or blemish, “altogether lovely.”

Yet this negative praise, this bold denial of any fault, is far from expressing the fullness of the Church’s loving admiration. Jesus is positively lovely in her eyes. He is not merely good-looking or simply fair; His beauties are beauties that draw the heart, and His glories are the kind that charm it. Love looks out from those “dove’s eyes, washed with milk, and fitly set;” it flows from those “lips like lilies dropping sweet-smelling myrrh,” and it sparkles on those hands that are “full of gold rings, set with chrysolite.”

But although these words of the Church are the very peak of the language of praise, and were no doubt meant as the summit of all description, it is impossible for this one sentence, even when opened out by the most careful meditation, to express more than a tiny fragment of the admiration she feels. Like one of the sons of Anak, this sentence towers over all others; but even its height falls short of the towering height of love born in heaven. It is only a faint symbol of an affection beyond words, a choice pearl washed ashore from the deep sea of love.

The Lord’s Jewels

Goldsmiths make exquisite shapes out of precious material; they fashion bracelets and rings from gold. God makes His precious things out of worthless material. From the black pebbles of polluted brooks He has picked up stones and set them in the golden ring of His unchanging love, to make them gems that will sparkle on His finger forever.

Beauty in Christ

There is something called beauty that wins people’s hearts. Many mighty men have bowed before it and paid it homage. But if you want true beauty, look into the face of Jesus, for there all loveliness is concentrated. There is no beauty anywhere except in Christ. O sun, you are not fair once you are compared with Him. O fair world, grand creation of a glorious God, you are only a dim, dusky smudge compared with the splendours of His face. When we see Christ, we will have to say that we never knew what loveliness was before. When the clouds are swept away and the curtains that hide Him from our view are drawn back, we will find that nothing we have ever seen or heard of in the whole wide universe, however grand or graceful, will stand a moment’s comparison with Him who was once seen as a root out of dry ground, but will soon fill heaven and earth with splendour and gladden every heart with His glory.

Love to Christ

Do you have a friend at court, at heaven’s court? Is the Lord Jesus your friend? Can you say that you love Him, and has He ever revealed Himself to you in love? Oh, to be able to say, “Christ is my friend,” is one of the sweetest things in the world. The love of Christ does not drive out love for our family; it makes our human love holy and far sweeter. Earthly love is sweet, but it must pass away. And what will you do when death comes, if you have no wealth but the wealth that fades and no love but the love that dies? Oh, to have the love of Christ! You can take that across the river of death with you. You can wear it as your jewel in heaven and set it as a seal on your hand, for His love is “strong as death, and mightier than the grave.”

Love’s Widening Circles

The Christian’s sympathy should always be as wide as possible, because he serves a God of infinite love. When grace throws the precious stone of love into the crystal pool of a renewed heart, it stirs the clear waters of life into ever-widening circles of sympathy. The first ring is not very wide: we love our household, for anyone who does not care for his own household is worse than a pagan. But look at the next ring around it: we love the household of faith. “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.” Look once more, for the ever-widening ring has reached the very edge of the lake and taken in everything within it, for “supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks are to be made for all men.” A follower of Jesus means a friend of humanity. A Christian is a philanthropist by profession and generous by the power of grace. His love stretches as far as sorrow reigns, and where he cannot help, he still feels pity.

The Condescension of Christ

When the Saviour appeared among us, it was not as someone raised from the ranks to win a position for Himself, but as someone who came down from heaven to bring blessings to the people. The ignorant and uneducated find in Him their best friend. He is no stern lawgiver, wrapped up in His own integrity, looking at the wrongdoer with the eye of justice. Nor is He simply the bold announcer of penalty and punishment, or the pitiless denouncer of crime and wickedness. He is the gentle lover of our souls, the good Shepherd who comes out not so much to kill the wolf as to save the sheep. As a nurse tenderly watches over her child, so He watches over people’s souls; and as a father pities his children, so Jesus pities poor sinners. It is not so much a matter of drawing sinners up to Him as of coming down to them; not standing on the mountaintop and telling them to climb, but coming down from the mountain and mixing with them as one of them; coming down from the high pastures after His sheep in the glens and ravines, so that He can take hold of them, lift them onto His mighty shoulders and carry them up to the place where He will fold them in purity, bless them with all grace and keep them for the glory to come.

fields.title: Grace and Salvation
fields.body_html:
The Triumph of Grace

It is one of the greatest wonders that not everyone loves Christ. Nothing shows more clearly how utterly corrupt our race is than the fact that “He was despised and rejected of men.” Yet those who have seen the fountains of the great deep of human depravity broken open have no trouble explaining how the Messiah was treated. Darkness could not have fellowship with light, nor Christ with Belial. Fallen humanity could not walk with Jesus, because the two were not agreed. When two such opposites met, it was the inevitable result that the guilty creature should hate the Perfect One. “Crucify Him, crucify Him,” is the natural cry of fallen man. Our first wonder is pushed aside, and another fills our thoughts. Were we amazed that not everyone loves Him? It is a greater marvel still that anyone loves Jesus. In the first case we saw the terrible blindness that could not see the brightness of the sun; we saw it with a shudder and were greatly astonished. But in this second case we see Jesus of Nazareth opening the tight-shut eye and scattering the Egyptian darkness with the Divine radiance of His marvellous light. Is this any less a wonder? If it was strange to see the dreadful ravings of the demon-possessed man among the tombs, it is surely far more astonishing to see that same man sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind. It is truly a triumph of grace when a human heart is brought to give its love to Jesus, for it proves that Satan’s work is all undone and that the person has been restored from the fallen state.

The Robe of Righteousness

Our formal dress for heaven’s court, and our garment of holiness for everyday wear, are gifts that Christ’s love stooped to give.

The Gospel

Everything you need is in the gospel. Do you need something to hold you up in trouble? It is in the gospel: “As thy days, so shall thy strength be.” Do you need something to steel you for duty? There is all-sufficient grace for everything God calls you to bear or to achieve. Do you need something to light up the eye of your hope? Oh, there are flashes of joy in the gospel that make your eye flash back the undying fires of bliss. Do you want something to help you stand firm in the middle of temptation? In the gospel there is what can make you immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord. There is no passion, no affection, no thought, no wish, no power that the gospel has not filled to the brim. The gospel was clearly made for human beings; it fits them in every part. There is knowledge for the head, love for the heart and guidance for the feet.

Love Undeserved

Nothing makes a person love Christ so much as a sense of His love weighed against a sense of how unworthy we are of it. It is sweet to think that Christ loves us; but oh, to remember that we are black as the “tents of Kedar,” and still He loves us! That is a thought that may well wean us from everything else.

Grace

Grace is always grace, but it never seems so gracious as when we see it brought to our own unworthy selves.

Vessels of Mercy

God’s chosen ones are called “vessels of mercy.” Now we know that a vessel is nothing but a receiver. A “vessel” is not a fountain, only a container that holds what is poured into it. So it is with God’s redeemed. By nature they are not fountains from which anything good springs up; they are simply receivers. At one time they are full of themselves, but grace empties them, and then as empty vessels they are set in the path of God’s goodness. God fills them to the brim with His loving-kindness, and so they are shown to be the vessels of His mercy. As “vessels” they may afterward pour out to others, but they can only pour out what God has put in them. They may work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, but they cannot work it out unless God works in them both to will and to do His good pleasure. They may overflow with gratitude, but only because God has filled them with grace. They may stream with holiness, but only because the Lord keeps the supply overflowing. They are receivers, and receivers only.

The Gospel Requirement

The gospel is not a plan for giving to God, but for receiving from God. It is taking from His fullness, drinking from His “wells of salvation,” receiving from His storehouse. Sinner, remember that all God asks of you for your salvation is that you be a receiver; and He gives you even this, the power to receive. He does not ask you to do anything, but to hold out your empty hand and take everything you need. He does not tell you to fill your barns and become rich; He tells you simply to confess your poverty and open the doors of your empty rooms, so that He may pour out such a blessing on you that you will hardly find room to hold it. Have you learned this truth? Have you come to live as a receiver from God’s hand? Have you stood at Mercy’s gate, humbly seeking salvation? For if you have not, if you have never yet been willing to take the riches of grace from God instead of giving Him your own worthless deeds, if you are not willing to receive His free goodness, you are a complete stranger to anything like the gospel of Christ.

Grace Abounds Much More

There has never been a time in this world’s history when it was entirely given over to sin. God has always had His servants on earth. At times they may have been hidden by fifties in the caves, but they have never been completely cut off. Grace may be low, and the stream very shallow, but it has never run entirely dry. The clouds have never been so widespread as to hide the day. But the time is fast approaching when grace will spread over the whole world, and “the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.” “Grace doth much more abound;” and whatever the world has lost through sin, it has gained far more through grace. It is true that we have been driven out of a garden of delights, where peace, love and happiness had a glorious home; but through Jesus we have a fairer inheritance. The plains of heaven surpass the fields of paradise in the ever-new delights they give, while the tree of life and the river flowing from the throne make the people of heaven more than restored to paradise. It is true that through sin we have become subject to death; but has grace not revealed an immortality for whose sake we are glad to die? Life lost in Adam is more than restored in Christ. Adam tore our original robes to pieces, but Jesus has clothed us with a divine righteousness worth far more than even the spotless robes of created innocence. We mourn our low and miserable condition through sin, but we rejoice at the thought that we are now more secure than before we fell; we are brought into a closer bond with Jesus than our standing as mere creatures could ever have claimed. O Jesus, You have won us an inheritance wider than Adam ever lost. You have filled our treasure chest with greater riches than our sin ever squandered. You have loaded us with honours and given us privileges far finer than our natural birthright could ever have obtained. Truly, truly, “grace doth much more abound.”

All of Grace

After they are called by grace, God’s people are kept safe in Christ Jesus. They are “kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.” They are not allowed to sin away their eternal inheritance; as temptations arise, they are given strength to meet them, and as sin stains them, they are washed again and made clean once more. But notice: the reason God keeps His people is the same as the reason He made them His people, His own free, sovereign grace. If you have been rescued in the hour of temptation, stop and remember that you were not rescued for your own sake. There was nothing in you that deserved rescue. If you have been fed and supplied in your hour of need, it is not because you have been a faithful servant of God or a prayerful Christian; it is simply and only because of God’s mercy. Nothing He does for you is prompted by anything you do for Him; His reason for blessing you lies wholly and entirely in the depths of His own heart. Blessed be God, His people will be kept.

“Nor death nor hell shall e’er remove His favorites from His breast; In the dear bosom of His love They must forever rest.”

But why? Because they are holy? Because they are sanctified? Because they serve God with good works? No, but because He, in His sovereign grace, has loved them, does love them and will love them to the end. So salvation, from first to last, is all of grace. How humble, then, a Christian ought to be! We contribute nothing at all to our salvation; God has done it all. What we have received is undeserved mercy. It is His boundless, bottomless love that led Him to save us, and it is the same love and mercy that holds us up now. To Him be the glory!

This Man Receives Sinners

“This man receiveth sinners.” Poor sin-sick sinner, what a sweet word this is for you! Answer it, answer it, and say, “Surely, then, He will not reject me.” Let me encourage you to come to my Master, so that you may receive His great atonement and be clothed with all His righteousness. Note this: the people I am speaking to are the bona fide, real, actual sinners; not those who only say they are sinners in a general confession, but those who feel how lost, ruined and hopeless they are. All of these are openly and freely invited to come to Jesus Christ and be saved by Him. Come, poor sinner, come. Come, because He has said He will receive you. I know your fears. I know you say in your heart, “He will reject me. If I offer my prayer, He will not hear me; if I cry to Him, perhaps the heavens will be like brass. I have been such a great sinner that He will never take me into His house to live with Him.” Poor sinner, do not say so. He has published the decree. Is that not enough?
