He has said, “Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” Will you not risk yourself on that promise? Will you not go to sea in a ship as sound as this? He has said it. It has often been the saints’ only comfort; on this they have lived, and on this they have died. He has said it. What! Do you think Christ would tell you He will receive you and then not do it? Would He say, “Come ye to the supper,” and then shut the door on you? No. If He has said He will cast out no one who comes to Him, you can be sure He cannot, He will not, cast you out. Come, then, and test His love on this ground, that He has said it. Come, and do not be afraid. Remember, if you feel yourself to be a sinner, that feeling is God’s gift, so you may very safely come to One who has already done so much to draw you. If you feel your need of a Saviour, Christ made you feel it. If you have a wish to come after Christ, Christ gave you that wish. If you have any desire for God, God gave you that desire. If you can sigh for Christ, Christ made you sigh. If you can weep for Christ, Christ made you weep. Yes, even if you can only long for Him with the strong longing of someone who fears he can never find Him and yet hopes he may, if you can only hope for Him, He has given you that hope. And oh, will you not come to Him? You already have some of the King’s gifts on you; come and plead what He has done. No request can ever fail with God when you plead this. Come to Him, and you will find it is true, what is written, that “this man receiveth sinners.”

fields.title: Looking unto Jesus
fields.body_html:
Look Upwards

Christian, in all your troubles, look to God and be saved. In all your trials and afflictions, look to Christ and find deliverance. In all your anguish, in all your repentance for your guilt, look to Christ and find pardon. Remember to lift your eyes toward heaven, and your heart toward heaven too. Wrap a golden chain around yourself and fasten one link of it to the staple in heaven. Look to Christ; do not be afraid. No one stumbles who walks with his eyes lifted to Jesus. Whoever looks at Christ walks safely.

Our Lord Jesus

Whatever blessed results flow from the perfect obedience, the finished atonement, the resurrection, ascension or intercession of the Lord Jesus, all of them are ours by His own gift. He now wears our names on His breastplate, and as He pleads with authority at the throne, He remembers us and pleads our cause. He uses the advantages of His high position, His rule over principalities and powers, and His absolute majesty in heaven for the good of those who trust in Him. His exalted state is as much at our service as His humbled state was. He who gave Himself for us in the depths of sorrow and death does not withdraw the gift now that He is enthroned in the highest heavens. Christ has no dignity He will not use to raise us up, and no right He will not exercise to defend us. Christ, everywhere and in every way, is our portion, to be enjoyed richly forever and ever.

The Intercession of Christ

The Lord Jesus has led captivity captive, and now sits at the right hand of God, forever interceding for us. Can your faith picture Him? Like a Levitical high priest of old, He stands with arms outstretched. There is majesty in His bearing, and He pleads with authority. On His head is the bright, shining turban of His priesthood, and on His chest glitter the precious stones on which the names of His people are engraved forever. Listen as He pleads. Can you not hear what it is? Is that your prayer He is mentioning before the throne? The prayer you offered this morning, Christ is now offering before His Father’s throne. The promise you made just now, He is now speaking there. He is the Altar and the Priest, and He perfumes our prayers with His own sacrifice. And yet perhaps you have been praying a long time and had no answer. Poor weeping petitioner, you have sought the Lord and He has not seemed to hear you, or at least has not answered you in a way that delights your soul, and you are full of darkness and heaviness because of it. “Look to Him, and be lightened.” If you do not succeed, He will. If your intercession goes unnoticed, His cannot be passed over. Your prayers may be like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again, but His prayers are not like that. He is God’s Son; He pleads, and He must prevail. God cannot refuse His own Son what He now asks, He who once bought mercies with His blood. Oh, take heart; keep on praying, for Jesus “ever liveth to make intercession” for you.

A View of Christ

A sight of Christ always does a Christian good. We cannot have too much of Christ; there can be no needless repetition when His name is mentioned. Give us Christ always, Christ forever. The sameness of Christ is a sweet variety, and even the oneness of Christ holds all the elements of harmony. Christ on His cross and on His throne, in the manger and in the tomb: Christ everywhere is sweet to us. We love His name, we adore His person, we delight to hear of His works; the theme is always new.

Some complain that their love for the Saviour is faint and cold. But this would not be so if they spent more time with Jesus. The closer you live to Christ, and the better you know Him, the more you will love Him. Do not try to produce a certain amount of love for Christ in yourself by some extraordinary means. Go into His presence, meditate on Him continually, picture His sufferings for you, and then you will love Him. It will become easy, because as you think about Him like this, He will draw your poor heart closer to Himself; and your love for Him will grow in exact proportion as you grasp His love for you.

Seeking Christ

Waiting soul, consider that this mercy is worth waiting for. Is it not salvation, your soul’s deliverance from hell? A long wait at the gate of mercy will be well repaid if the King at last gives you this jewel of surpassing worth.

Think, too, how utterly unworthy of this mercy you are; so do not be reluctant to humble yourself, or to wait patiently on the sovereign will of Jehovah. Proud people must be noticed at once, or they will leave; but you have nothing to boast of, and you should feel that if He disregarded you for a long time, your unworthiness could not demand any apology for His delay. Remember too that He will hear at last. His promise would be broken if one praying soul could perish, for He has said, “Seek, and ye shall find”; “Whosoever calleth on the name of the Lord shall be saved.” The delay may be for your good, to lay you lower in the dust of humility, or to make you more earnest for the blessing. Perhaps the Lord means to test your faith, so that, like the Syrophoenician woman, you may bring Him honour by your confidence in Him. Keep praying, for “the Lord is good unto them that wait for Him, to the soul that seeketh Him.”

Consider Him

Believer, weary and disheartened by the roughness of the road, look at the Master’s footprints, and see how He suffered. You are tested and troubled, and you ask for comfort. What better comfort could you have than the fact that Jesus Christ shares your nature; that He has suffered everything you are suffering now; that His holy feet walked your path before you; that the cup you are drinking is a cup He drained to the very bottom; that the river you are crossing is one He swam through, and every wave and breaker rolling over your head once rolled over Him? Come, are you ashamed and unwilling to suffer what your Master suffered? Is the disciple to be above his Master, and the servant above his Lord? Is He to die on a cross, and you not carry the cross? Must He be crowned with thorns, and you crowned with laurel? Is He to be pierced in His hands and feet, and His followers to feel no pain? Oh, throw away this foolish illusion. Look to Him who “endured the cross, despising the shame,” and be ready to endure and suffer just as He did. You have His example to guide you and His sympathy to cheer you.

The Holy Saviour

The apostle Paul uses a very beautiful and meaningful expression about the Lord Jesus: “who knew no sin.” It does not simply say He did none, but that He knew none. Sin was no acquaintance of His. He was acquainted with grief, but He was no acquaintance of sin. He had to walk among its busiest haunts, yet He did not know it. It is not that He was ignorant of its nature or unaware of its penalty, but He did not know it; He was a stranger to it. Never by word, nod or smile did He give it the faintest recognition. Of course He knew what sin was, for He was truly God; but with sin He had no communion, no fellowship, no kinship. He was a complete stranger in the presence of sin, a foreigner, not a citizen of the land where sin is recognized. He passed through the wilderness of suffering, but He could never go into the wilderness of sin. “He knew no sin.” Note that expression and treasure it; and when you think of your Substitute and see Him bleeding on the cross, imagine that you see written in those lines of blood, “He knew no sin.” Mixed with the redness of His blood, that Rose of Sharon, see the purity of His nature, the Lily of the Valley: “He knew no sin.”

Christ our Example

Remember the blessed example of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Surely this will teach you not to live for yourself! “For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor, that we through His poverty might be rich.” His heart is made of tenderness; His inmost being melts with love. In all our afflictions He is afflicted. Ever since the day He became flesh of our flesh, He has never hidden Himself from our sufferings. Our glorious Head is moved by every sorrow that troubles the members. Crowned though He now is, He does not forget the thorns He once wore. Amid the splendours of His royal state in Paradise, He does not forget His children here below. He is still persecuted when Saul persecutes the saints; His brothers and sisters are still the apple of His eye and very near His heart. If you can find a grain of selfishness in Christ, then devote yourselves to your lusts and let Mammon be your god. If you can find in Christ a single atom of hardness of heart or callousness of spirit, then justify yourselves, you whose hearts are stone to the cries of the desolate. But if you claim to be followers of the Man of Nazareth, be full of compassion. He feeds the hungry so that they do not faint on the way; He binds up the broken-hearted and heals all their wounds; He hears the cry of the needy and rises to help them. If you are His disciples, go and do the same.

Look to Christ

Do you want to be free from doubts? Do you want to rejoice in the Lord with unmoved faith and unshaken confidence? Then look to Jesus! I am certain that if we lived more with Jesus, were more like Jesus and trusted more in Jesus, doubts and fears would be very scarce and rare.

A Complete Saviour

It would not fit the character of Him “by whom are all things” if He had sent an incomplete Saviour, that is, if He had left us to do part ourselves and Christ to do the rest. Look at the sun. God wills the sun to light the earth; does He ask the earth’s darkness to contribute to the light? Does He question the night and ask whether it has something in its gloomy shadows to add to the brightness of noon? No. Up rises the sun in the morning like a giant to run his race, and the earth is made bright. And will God turn to the dark sinner and ask whether there is anything in him that could contribute to eternal light? No. Jesus rises as the Sun of Righteousness, with healing in His wings, and at His coming darkness becomes light. He alone is “the light of the world.” His own arm brought salvation. He asks no help from anyone, but gives everything and does everything out of His own rich grace, and He is a complete and perfect Saviour.

fields.title: The Joy of the Christian Life
fields.body_html:
A Rich Life

Old chroniclers say that when one of our kings came home from captivity, the fountains in Cheapside ran with wine. The king was so generous and the people so glad that instead of water they let wine flow freely for everyone. There is a way of making our life so rich, so full and such a blessing to others that the picture may fit us too, and people may say that our life flows with wine while other lives flow with water. You have known some people like that. John Howard’s life was not like our poor, ordinary lives; he was so kind, and his sympathy for humanity so self-denying, that the streams of his life were like generous wine. Perhaps you have known personally some outstanding saint, someone who lived very near to Jesus. When he spoke, there was an anointing and a flavour about his words, a solidity and strength in what he said, that you could appreciate though you could not reach it yourself. You have sometimes said, “I wish my words were as full, as sweet, as mellow and as rich as that person’s words. Oh, I wish my actions were as rich, as deep in colour and as pure in taste as the actions of someone else you point to. Everything I can do seems small and empty next to his high attainments. Oh, that I could do more! Oh, that I could send streams of pure gold into every house, instead of my poor dross!” Well, Christian, this should spur you on to keep your heart full of rich things. Never, ever neglect the Word of God. It will make your heart rich with instruction, your head rich with understanding, and your inmost being rich with compassion. Then your conversation, as it flows from your mouth, will come from your soul and, like everything inside you, will be rich, warm and full of savour. Only let your heart be full of sweet, generous love, and the stream that flows from your lips will be sweet and generous. Above all, have Jesus living in your heart, and then rivers of living water will flow out of you, more refreshing, purer and more satisfying than the water of the well at Sychar that Jacob drank from. Go with Christian to the great mine of unsearchable riches, and cry to the Holy Spirit to make your heart rich toward salvation. Then your life and conversation will be a gift to those around you; and when they see you, your face will shine, and your face will be like the face of an angel of God.

A Full Heart

You have seen the great reservoirs our water companies provide, where water is stored to supply thousands of houses. Well, the heart is a person’s reservoir, from which the streams of his life flow.

That life may flow through different pipes, the mouth, the hand, the eye; but everything that comes from hand, eye and lip has its source in the great fountain and central reservoir, the heart. So it is easy to show how necessary it is to keep this reservoir in good condition, since otherwise whatever flows through the pipes must be tainted and corrupt. The heart must not only be kept pure; it must also be kept full. However pure the water in the central reservoir, we cannot have a plentiful supply unless the reservoir itself is full. An empty fountain will certainly produce empty pipes. However precise the machinery, however well ordered everything else, if the reservoir is dry we may wait in vain for water. See, then, how necessary it is to keep the heart full; and let that need make you ask: “But how can I keep my heart full? How can my feelings be strong? How can I keep my desires burning and my zeal ablaze?” Christian, there is one text that explains it all: “All my springs are in Thee,” said David. If all your springs are in God, your heart will be full enough. If you go to the foot of Calvary, your heart will be bathed there in love and gratitude. If you are often in the valley of solitude, talking with your God, your heart will be full of calm resolve. If you go with your Master to the Mount of Olives to weep with Him over Jerusalem, your heart will be full of love for undying souls. If you are continually drawing your motivation, your life, your whole being from the Holy Spirit, without whom you can do nothing, and if you are living in close communion with Christ, there is no danger of your heart running dry. The one who lives without prayer, or with little prayer, who seldom reads the Word, who seldom looks up to heaven for fresh power from above, is the one whose heart will become dry and barren. But the one who calls on his God in secret, who spends much time in holy solitude, who delights to meditate on the words of the Most High, whose soul is given over to Christ, who delights in His fullness, rejoices in His all-sufficiency, prays for His second coming and delights in the thought of His glorious return, must have an overflowing heart; and as his heart is, so his life will be. It will be a full life, a life that will speak from the grave and wake the echoes of the future. “Keep thine heart with all diligence,” and beg the Holy Spirit to keep it full; otherwise what flows from your life will be feeble, shallow and superficial, and you might as well not have lived at all.

Oh, for a heart like that, full and deep and broad! Find someone with such a heart, and that is the person from whom living waters will flow to gladden the world with their refreshing streams.

The Happiness of Religion

Let someone truly know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he will be a happy person; and the more deeply he drinks of the Spirit of Christ, the happier he will become. A religion that teaches misery as a duty is plainly false, for when God made the world He planned for the happiness of His creatures. As you look at everything around you, you cannot help thinking that God has carefully, with the closest attention, looked for ways to please us. He has not just given us the bare necessities; He has given us more, not only the useful but even the beautiful. The flowers in the hedgerow, the stars in the sky, the beauties of nature, hill and valley: all these were made not only because we needed them, but because God wanted to show how He loved us and how much He wanted us to be happy. Now it is not likely that the God who made a happy world would send a miserable salvation. He who is a happy Creator will be a happy Redeemer; and those who have tasted that the Lord is gracious can testify that the ways of true religion “are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.” And if this life were all, if death were the burial of our whole life and the shroud the winding-sheet of eternity, it would still be a bright and happy thing to be a Christian, for it lights up this valley of tears and fills the wells in the valley of Baca to the brim with streams of love and joy.

Faith—a Present Joy

True religion has its present joys. Speak, you who know them, for you can tell of them, though you cannot list them all. Oh, would you give up your faith for all the joys the world calls good or great? Tell me, if your immortal life could be snuffed out, would you give it up even for all the kingdoms of this world? You who are poor, has this not been a candle to you in the darkness? Has it not given you light through the heavy shadows of your troubles? You who toil, has this not been your rest, your sweet repose? Have God’s testimonies not been your song in the house of your pilgrimage? You children of sorrow, racked with pain, has your faith not been a sweet quietus in your sufferings? Is faith not worth having in the sickroom? And you business people, speak for yourselves. You have hard struggles to get through life. Sometimes you have been driven to the very edge, and whether you would succeed or not seemed to hang by a thread. Has your faith not been a joy to you in your difficulties? Has it not calmed your minds? When you have been fretted and troubled about worldly things, have you not found it pleasant to go into your room, shut the door and tell your Father in secret all your cares? And you who are rich, can you not give the same testimony, if you have loved the Master? What would all your riches have been to you without a Saviour? Can you not say that your faith gilded your gold and made your silver shine more brightly? For everything you have is sweetened by the thought that you have all these things and Christ too. Was there ever a child of God who could deny this? We have heard of many unbelievers who grieved over their unbelief when they came to die. Did you ever hear of anyone on his deathbed looking back with sorrow on a life of holiness? Never, never have we known a Christian who regretted being a Christian. We have seen Christians suffering so much that we wondered how they lived; so poor that we wondered at their hardship; so full of doubts that we pitied their unbelief; but we never heard them say, even then, “I regret that I gave myself to Christ.” No; with the clasp of the dying, when heart and flesh were failing, we have seen them hug this treasure to their chest and press it to their heart, still feeling that this was their life, their joy, their all. Oh, if you want to be happy, if you want to be saved, if you want to scatter sunshine on your path, dig out the nettles and blunt the thorns, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and His righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” Do not seek happiness first; seek Christ first, and happiness will follow. Seek the Lord first, and then He will provide for you in this life and crown it with everything glorious in the life to come.

Joy Over the Repenting

The angels know what the joys of heaven are, and that is why they rejoice over one sinner who repents. We talk about pearly gates and golden streets, white robes, harps of gold and crowns of amaranth; but if an angel could speak to us about heaven, he would smile and say, “All these fine things are only child’s talk. You are little children, and you cannot understand the greatness of eternal bliss. So God has given you a child’s primer and an alphabet in which you can learn the first rough letters of what heaven is; but what it is you do not know. Mortal, your eye has never yet seen its splendours; your ear has never yet been enchanted by its melodies; your heart has never been carried away by its matchless joys.” Yes, we may talk and think and guess and dream, but we can never measure the infinite heaven God has prepared for His children. But the angels know its glory; and that is one reason they rejoice over the repenting sinner who has now become heir to such an inheritance.

Untiring Delight

Who has ever called the sea monotonous? Even for the sailor, crossing it as he does, sometimes for a year at a time, there is always freshness in the rise and fall of the waves, the whiteness of the breaker’s foam, the curl of the crested wave and the playful chase of every wave by its long train of brothers. Which of us has ever complained that the sun gives us little variety? What if every morning he harnesses the same horses and flashes the same golden glory from his chariot, climbs with dull sameness to the top of the sky, then drives his chariot down again and bids his flaming horses cool their burning hooves in the western sea? Or who among us would complain in disgust that the bread we eat has grown tiresome to the taste? We eat it today, tomorrow and the next day; we have eaten it for years past; still the same unchanging food is served on the table, and bread remains the staff of life. Translate these earthly experiences into heavenly mysteries. If Christ is your food and your spiritual bread, if Christ is your sun, your heavenly light, if Christ is the sea of love in which your passions swim and all your joys are found, then it is impossible for you as Christians to complain of monotony in Him. “He is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever;” and yet He has the “dew of His youth.” He is like the manna in the golden jar, which was always the same; but He is also like the manna that came down from heaven new every morning. He is like the rod of Moses, which was dry and never changed its shape; but He is also to us like the rod of Aaron, which buds and blossoms and produces almonds.

The Joy of Pardon

Oh, what a joyful thing it is to have a ray of heavenly sunlight in the soul, and to hear the very voice of God as He walks in the garden of our souls in the cool of the day, saying to us, “Son, thy sins which are many, are all forgiven thee.” The whisper of that heavenly voice can lift our hearts to an almost divine bliss. It gives a joy that all the pleasures, riches and enjoyments this world can offer cannot equal. To have the divine kiss of acceptance, to be clothed in the best robe, to wear the ring on the hand and the sandals on the feet, to hear the heavenly music and dancing with which returning prodigals are welcomed to their Father’s house: this is truly a bliss and blessedness worth whole worlds to experience.

True Blessing

When Christ blesses, He blesses not only in word but in deed. The lips of truth cannot promise more than the hands of love will certainly give.

Needless Poverty

Many a believer lives in the cottage of doubt when he could live in the mansion of faith.

The Spirit of Praise

“Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless His holy name.” Wake up, my memory, and find material for the song. Tell what God has done for me in days gone by. Fly back, my thoughts, to my childhood, and sing of the mercies of the cradle. Look back over my youth and its early kindnesses. Sing of the patient grace that followed my wanderings and put up with my rebellions. Bring before my eyes that glad hour when I first knew the Lord, and tell again the matchless story of His mercy. Wake up, my judgment, and give the music its measure. Come out, my understanding, and weigh His loving-kindness on the scales. See if you can count the fine dust of His mercies. See if you can estimate the unsearchable riches God has given you in His indescribable gift of Christ Jesus. Recount His eternal love for you. Add up the treasures of that everlasting covenant He made on your behalf, which was “ordered in all things and sure.” Sing aloud of the divine wisdom that devised, the love that planned and the grace that carried out the plan of your redemption. “Bless the Lord, O my soul!” For does not all nature around me praise Him? If I were silent, I would be the one exception in the universe. Does the thunder not praise Him as it rolls like drums in the march of the God of Armies? Do the mountains not praise Him when the woods on their summits sway in worship? Does the lightning not write His name in letters of fire on the midnight darkness? Has the whole earth not got a voice? And shall I, can I, be silent? “Bless the Lord, O my soul.”

Strength through Joy

When the mind is happy, it can work hard. “The joy of the Lord is your strength.”

Rejoice Always

Whenever a Christian gives way to a gloomy, despondent spirit in his trials; when he does not seek grace from God to fight trouble bravely and cheerfully; when he does not ask his heavenly Father for the strength and comfort that will enable him to rejoice in the Lord at all times, he dishonours the high, mighty and noble principles of Christianity, which are made to hold a person up and make him happy even in times of the deepest affliction. It is the boast of the gospel that it lifts the heart above trouble. It is one of the glories of our faith that it makes us say, “Although the fig-tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vine, the labor of the olive shall fail, and the field shall yield no meat, yet will I rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”

Christian Gladness

David was as outstanding for the joy and gladness of his heart as he was for his godliness. Worldly people often think that thinking about divine things tends to depress the spirits. There is no greater mistake. No one is so happy that he would not be happier still with true religion. The person who has a fullness of earthly pleasure would not lose any part of his happiness if he had the grace of God in his heart. Instead, that joy would add sweetness to all his prosperity; it would strain many bitter dregs out of his cup and show him how to draw more honey from the honeycomb. Godliness can make the most melancholy joyful, and it can make joyful people more joyful still, lighting up the face with heavenly gladness and making the eyes sparkle ten times more brightly. However happy the worldly person may be, he will find there is a sweeter nectar than any he has drunk before if he comes to the fountain of atoning mercy, if he knows that his name is written in the book of everlasting life. Then his earthly mercies will have the charm of redemption to make them richer. They will no longer be like shadowy phantoms that dance for a passing hour in the sunbeam. He will count them more precious because they are given to him, as it were, in some codicils of the divine will, which has promise for the life that now is as well as for the life to come. While goodness and mercy follow him all the days of his life, he will be able to look forward gratefully to the future when he will live in the house of the Lord forever, and to say with the Psalmist, “Thou hast made me most blessed forever: Thou hast made me exceeding glad with Thy countenance.”

In This You Greatly Rejoice

“Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness.” Can a Christian “greatly rejoice” while he is “in heaviness”? Yes, he most certainly can. Sailors tell us that in some parts of the sea there is a strong current on the surface going one way, while down in the depths a strong current runs the other way. The two do not meet or interfere with one another; one stream of water on the surface runs in one direction, and another below runs in the opposite direction. The Christian is like that. On the surface there is a stream of heaviness rolling in dark waves, but down in the depths there is a strong undercurrent of great rejoicing that always flows. Do you ask what causes this great rejoicing? The apostle tells us: “Wherein ye greatly rejoice.” What does he mean? Look at his letter and you will see. He is writing “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, etc.” And the first thing he says to them is that they are “elect according to the foreknowledge of God.” This is an assurance “wherein ye greatly rejoice.” Even when the Christian is most “in heaviness through manifold temptations,” what a mercy it is that he can know he is still chosen by God! Anyone who is sure that God “has chosen him from before the foundation of the world” may well say, “Wherein I greatly rejoice.” Let us think about this. Before God made the heavens and the earth, or set the pillars of the sky in their golden sockets, He set His love on me. He wrote my name on the chest of the great High Priest, and it stands in His everlasting book, never to be erased: “elect according to the foreknowledge of God.” Why, this can make a person’s soul leap within him, and all the heaviness that the weaknesses of the flesh may lay on him will be as nothing. For this tremendous current of His overflowing joy will sweep away the mill-dam of his grief. Bursting through and leaping over every obstacle, it will flood over all his sorrows until they are drowned and covered, never to be mentioned again. “Wherein ye greatly rejoice.” Come, Christian, you are depressed and downcast. Think for a moment: you are chosen by God and precious. Let the bell of election ring in your ear, that ancient Sabbath bell of the covenant; let your name be heard in its notes. And tell me, I beg you, tell me, does this not make you “greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, thou art in heaviness through manifold temptations?”

You will see another reason too. The apostle says we are “elect through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”: “wherein we greatly rejoice.” Is the obedience of the Lord Jesus Christ wrapped around me as my beauty and my glorious clothing? Is the blood of Jesus sprinkled on me to take away all my guilt and all my sin? And shall I not greatly rejoice in this? What could there be in all the low spirits that may come over me that would make me break my harp, even if for a moment I hang it on the willows? Do I not expect my songs to rise to heaven once again? And even now, through the thick darkness, do the sparks of my joy not appear when I remember that the blood of Jesus is still on me and the glorious righteousness of the Messiah is still around me?

But the apostle’s great and cheering comfort is that we are chosen for “an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for us,” just as we are kept for it. This may well make the believer greatly rejoice. He is drawing near the gates of death, and his spirit is heavy, because he has to leave behind everything that life holds dear. Besides, illness naturally brings low spirits with it. But you sit with him in his room and begin to talk to him about the

“Sweet fields beyond the swelling flood, Arrayed in living green.”

You tell him of Canaan on the other side of the Jordan, of the land flowing with milk and honey, of the Lamb in the middle of the throne and of all the glories God has prepared for those who love Him; and you see his dull eye light up with angelic brightness. “His heaviness” is all gone, and the language of his heart is—

“On Jordan’s stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye To Canaan’s fair and happy land, Where my possessions lie.”

Looking forward to the coming glory and happiness fills him with “joy unspeakable.”

fields.title: Prayer
fields.body_html:
Persevering Prayer

Do not give up the prayers God’s Spirit has put in your heart, for remember, the things you have asked for are worth waiting for. Besides, when you pray you are a beggar, so you must not be a chooser about when God will hear you. If you had a right view of yourself, you would say, “It is a wonder He ever listens to me at all, unworthy as I am. Does the Infinite really bend His ear to me? May I hope He will listen to me in the end? Then I may well keep on praying.”

And remember, it is your only hope: there is no other Saviour. This or nothing: Christ’s blood or else eternal wrath. And who will you go to if you turn away from Him? No one has ever perished while pleading for mercy, so keep on.

Besides, better people than you have had to wait. Kings and patriarchs and prophets have waited, so surely you can be content to sit in the King’s waiting room for a little while. It is an honour to sit at the gate as Mordecai did. Keep praying; keep waiting!

“Ah,” someone says, “that is exactly what I have been doing for a long time.” Yes, yes, but there are different kinds of waiting. A man says, “I have been waiting,” but he has folded his arms and gone to sleep. You may wait like that until you are lost. The waiting I mean is “getting everything ready”: the waiting of a poor sufferer for the doctor, who cries out in pain, “Is the doctor coming?” I will stand guarantee for my Master when I say that no one like that will be sent away empty. He will never break His promise. Try Him, try Him!

Believing Prayer

Prayers are heard in heaven very much in proportion to our faith. Little faith will get very great mercies, but great faith will get greater still. In the old days it was the custom for all the poor in the parish to call at every house with bowls for food, and whatever size the bowl was, every generous person would fill it. Faith is our bowl. If we have only “little faith,” we will get that filled; but if we have “great faith,” we will have that filled too. Little faith gets much; but great faith is a noble, princely merchant who does a great trade. It obtains millions where little faith gains only hundreds. Great faith gets hold of God’s treasure.

Continue in Prayer

Pray a great deal. God’s plants grow faster in the warm air of the place of prayer; it is a hothouse for spiritual growth. Whoever wants to grow strong must often kneel at the throne of grace. Of all the training for spiritual battles, knee training is the healthiest and most strengthening.

Unsubmissive Prayers

When we look at our prayers, we have good reason to regret the unsubmissive spirit that too often runs through them. How often in our prayers have we not simply wrestled with God for a blessing (that was allowed) but haughtily demanded it! We have not said, “Deny this to me, O my God, if that pleases You.” We have not been ready to say, as the Redeemer did, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as Thou wilt.” Instead we have asked according to the blind leanings of our ignorance, as if we could not bear to be refused by the all-knowing counsel of His will. Forgetting to defer humbly to our Lord’s greater wisdom and grace, we have asked and declared that we would not be satisfied unless we got the particular thing our hearts were set on. Now whenever we come to God and ask for something we think is truly good, we have every right to plead earnestly; but we go wrong when we go beyond earnestness and begin to demand. It is our part to ask for a blessing, but not to define what the blessing will be. It is our part to put our head under the mighty hands of divine blessing, but not to lift the hands, as Joseph did Jacob’s, and say, “Not so, my father.” We must be content if He gives the blessing with crossed hands, just as content for Him to put His left hand on our head as His right. We must not push our way into God’s storehouse of gifts. “It is the Lord, let Him do as seemeth Him good.” Prayer was never meant to put a chain on God’s sovereignty. We must always add this heavenly postscript at the bottom of our prayer: “Father, deny this if that is most for Your glory.” Christ will have nothing to do with dictating prayers.

fields.title: Holiness and the New Life
fields.body_html:
Faith a Personal Matter

Some people say they will test the holiness of Christ’s religion by the holiness of Christ’s people. I reply that you have no right to put the question to any such test. The proper test is to try it yourselves, to “taste and see that the Lord is good.” By tasting and seeing you will prove His goodness, and in the same way you must prove the holiness of His Gospel. Your business is to seek Christ crucified for yourselves, not to accept someone else’s account of the power of grace to overcome corruption and make the heart holy. Since God has given you a Bible, He meant you to read it, not to be content with reading people. You are not to be content with feelings stirred up by other people’s conversation. The only way you can know true religion is by having His Holy Spirit at work on your own heart, so that you experience its power for yourself. You have no right to judge religion by anything outside it. And if you despise it before you have tried it yourself, you must stand convicted as a fool in this world and as a criminal in the next. And yet this is how it is with most people. If you hear someone rail at the Bible, you can usually conclude that he never reads it. And if you hear someone speak against true religion, you can be quite sure he never knew what it was. True religion, once it takes hold of the heart, never lets a person quarrel with it. Anyone who knows Christ at all will call Christ his best friend. We have found many who despised the pleasures of this world, but we never found one who turned away from true religion in disgust or weariness after once enjoying it. No, no! You chose your own delusions, and you chose them at your own risk; you cling to them at your own peril. For if you take your religion from other people and are led by the example of those who profess it to throw religion away, you are still guilty of your own blood. God has not left you to the unreliable chart of other people’s characters. He has given you His own Word, the more sure word of testimony, to which you do well to pay attention.

Holiness

Holiness is the architect’s plan by which God builds up His living temple.

The New Heart

God does not promise to improve our nature or to mend our broken hearts. No; the promise is that He will give us new hearts and right spirits. Human nature is too far gone ever to be mended. It is not a house slightly in need of repair, with a slate blown off the roof here and a piece of plaster fallen from the ceiling there. No, it is rotten all through. The very foundations have been undermined. There is not one sound timber in it. It is all rotten from the top of the roof to the bottom of the foundation, and ready to fall. God does not try to mend it. He does not prop up the walls and repaint the door; He does not decorate and beautify it. He decides that the old house will be swept away entirely and that He will build a new one. It is too far gone to be mended. If it were only a little in need of repair, it might be restored. If only a wheel or two of that great thing called “Manhood” were broken, then He who made man might put it all right. He might put in a new cog where one had snapped off, and another wheel where one had worn out, and the machine might run again. But no; the whole thing is broken. There is not one lever that is not broken, not one axle that is not out of place. “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is faint. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, it is wounds, and bruises, and putrefying sores.” So the Lord does not try to repair it, but says, “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”

Christ in You

What does it mean to have “Christ in you”? The Roman Catholic hangs the cross on his chest; the true Christian carries the cross in his heart. And a cross inside the heart is one of the sweetest cures for a cross on the back. If you have a cross in your heart, Christ crucified in you, the hope of glory, the cross of this world’s troubles will seem light enough to you, and you will easily be able to carry it. Christ in the heart means Christ believed in, Christ loved, Christ trusted, Christ embraced as a bridegroom, Christ communed with, Christ as our daily food, and ourselves as the temple and palace where Jesus Christ walks every day. Ah, many are complete strangers to the meaning of this phrase. They do not know what it is to have Jesus Christ in them. Though they know a little about Christ on Calvary, they know nothing about Christ in the heart. Now remember: Christ on Calvary will save no one unless Christ is in the heart. The Son of Mary, born in the manger, will not save you unless He is also born in your heart and lives there as your joy, your strength and your comfort.

Life’s Great Object

As Christians, we ought always to stand out from the world in the great aim of our life. As for worldly people, some are seeking wealth, others fame; some seek comfort, others pleasure. In a lesser way you may seek any of these, but your main and chief motive as a Christian should always be to live for Christ. To live for glory? Yes, but for His glory. To live for comfort? Yes, but let all your comfort be in Him. To live for pleasure? Yes, but when you are merry, sing psalms and make music in your hearts to the Lord. To live for wealth? Yes, but to be rich in faith. You may store up treasure, but store it up in heaven, “where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.” You can make the most ordinary job truly sacred by dedicating your daily life entirely to the service of Jesus, taking as your motto, “For me to live is Christ.” It really is possible to live such a consecrated life; and if anyone denies it is possible, let them stand convicted by their own words, because they do not obey the command: “Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”

Faith a Present Concern

True religion must be a matter of the present, because the present is so closely bound up with the future. Scripture tells us that this life is seedtime and the future is harvest: “he that soweth to the flesh, shall of the flesh reap corruption; he that soweth to the spirit, shall of the spirit reap life everlasting.” Just as the seed produces the plant, this present life produces the eternal future. Heaven and hell are, after all, only the full development of our present character; for is it not written, “he that is holy, let him be holy still; he that is unjust, let him be unjust still”? Do we not know that condemnation lies sleeping in the heart of every sin? Is it not a fearful truth that the seed of everlasting torment lies dormant in every vile wish, every unholy thought, every unclean act? Hell, then, is only a great eruption of sleeping lava. It was so quiet that the mountain was covered with fair green growth right up to its summit, until death comes and tells the lava to rise, and the fiery lava of eternal misery pours down the slopes of a person’s eternal existence. Yet it was there before, for sin is hell, and rebellion against God is the prelude to misery. It is the same with heaven. I know that heaven is a reward not of debt but of grace; but still the Christian has something within him that gives him a foretaste of heaven. What did Christ say? “I give unto my sheep eternal life.” He did not say “I will give,” but “I do give.” As soon as they believe in Me, I give them eternal life. “He that believeth on Him that sent Me hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation.” The Christian has the seedbeds of a paradise within him. In due time the light sown for the righteous and the gladness sown for the upright in heart will spring up, and they will reap the harvest. Is it not plain, then, that true religion is something we must have here? Is it not clearly revealed that it matters for the present? For if this life is the seedtime of the future, how can I expect to reap any harvest in another world other than what I have been sowing here? How can I trust that I will be saved then unless I am saved now? How can I hope that heaven will be my eternal inheritance unless its first instalment has begun in my own soul on earth?

You Are Not Your Own

If you are a child of God, you belong wholly and entirely to Christ. Yet are there not many who seem to imagine that if they keep a corner of their souls for religion, all will be well? Satan may stride across the broad fields of their judgment and understanding, and rule over their thoughts and imaginations; but if the appearance of religion is kept up in some quiet corner, everything will be fine. Oh, do not be deceived about this. Christ has never yet gone halves in anyone. He will have the whole of you or none of you. He will be supreme Lord, highest Master, absolute King, or else He will have nothing to do with you. You may serve Satan if you want to, but when you serve him, you will not serve Christ too. If you are not wholly given up to God, if in the intention and purpose of your soul every thought and wish and power and talent and possession is not devoted and consecrated to Christ, you have no reason to believe you have been redeemed by His precious blood. In His people, whom He has bought for His own, He will reign without a rival. Christ will not be part-owner of anyone.

Nature and Grace

You will never see God in nature until you have learned to see God in grace. We have heard a great deal about rising from nature to nature’s God. Impossible! A man might as well try to go from the top of the Alps to heaven. To the natural mind there is still a great gulf between nature and God. You must first see God incarnate in the person of Christ before you will see God almighty in the creation He has made. You have heard a lot about people who love to worship in the forest glades but scorn to go to the sanctuary of the saints. Yes, but there was little truth in it. There is often a great noise where there is a great emptiness; and you will often find that the people who talk most about this natural worship are the ones who do not worship God at all. God’s works are too coarse a medium to let the light through. The path is rugged and the air is dark if we try to find out the Creator fully by way of His creatures. But when I see Christ, I see God’s new and living way between my soul and my God, very clear and pleasant. I come to my God at once, and finding Him in Christ, I find Him everywhere else as well.

Evidence of the New Life

“If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious,” it is sure evidence of a divine change, for by nature people find no delight in Jesus. I do not ask what your experience may or may not have been. If Christ is precious to you, there has been a work of grace in your heart. If you love Him, if His presence is your joy, if His blood is your hope, if His glory is your goal and aim, and if His person is the constant love of your soul, you could not have had this taste by nature, for you were dead. You could not have acquired this taste by learning, for this is a miracle that only the God who is supreme over nature could have worked in you. Let every tested and troubled Christian who still tastes that the Lord is good take comfort from this. “The upright love thee.”

fields.title: Humility and Self-Examination
fields.body_html:
Humility

What is humility of mind? Humility is making a right estimate of yourself. It is not humility for someone to think less of himself than he ought, though he might find that rather hard to do. Some people tell you they cannot do something when they know they can; but surely you would not call that humility? Someone is asked to take part in some good work. “No,” he says, “I have no ability;” yet if you said that about him, he would be offended. It is not humility to stand up and run yourself down, saying you cannot do this, that or the other, when you know it is untrue. If God gives someone a talent, do you think that person does not know it? If someone has ten talents, he has no right to be dishonest with his Maker and say, “Lord, You have given me only five.” It is not humility to underrate your gifts. Humility is to think of yourself, if you can, as God thinks of you. It is to feel that if we have talents, God has given them to us, and to let it be seen that, like cargo in a ship, they tend to make us sit low. The more we have, the lower we ought to lie. Humility is not saying, “I do not have this gift;” it is saying, “I have the gift, and I must use it for my Master’s glory. I must never seek any honour for myself; for what do I have that I have not received?” Humility is feeling that we have no power of our own, but that it all comes from God. Humility is leaning on our Beloved and saying, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengtheneth me.” It is, in fact, to do away with self and to exalt the Lord Jesus Christ as All in All.

Self-Examination

“If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.” “If”: so it is possible that some may not have tasted that the Lord is gracious, and we need to ask whether we are among those who know the grace of God by experience of the heart. There is no spiritual revelation that may not call for searching the heart. At the very summit of holy delight we meet the challenge of the sentry “If”: “If ye then be risen with Christ.” And at the very bottom of the hill, even at Repentance Gate itself, He meets us with a warrant for arrest until He sees whether our sorrow is the godly sorrow that needs no regret. “If thou be the Son of God” is not always a temptation from the devil; it is often a very healthy question, quite rightly prompted by holy anxiety in people who want to build securely on the Rock of Ages. Even at the Lord’s Table it is right for us to pray, “Lord, is it I?” when there is a Judas among us; and after the most intimate fellowship Christ asked, “Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?” Do not let any enjoyment of the ordinances, or any high and rapturous fellowship we may have known, excuse us from the great duty of testing ourselves to see whether we are in the faith. So examine yourselves on this point, and do not rest content until you can say, “There is no ‘if’ about it; I have tasted that the Lord is gracious.”

The First Lesson

The doorstep of the temple of wisdom is knowing our own ignorance. No one can learn rightly who has not first been taught that he knows nothing. It is good for a person to feel that he is only beginning to learn, and to be willing to submit his heart to the teaching of God’s Spirit, so that he may be guided by Him in everything. The prayer of the soul brought to life is, “Teach thou me.” We become like little children when God begins to deal with us.

Danger of Prosperity

High places and God’s praise seldom go together. A full cup is not easily carried without spilling; whoever stands on a pinnacle needs a clear head and much grace.

The Right Estimate

The higher someone is in grace, the lower he will be in his own estimation.

Self

Faith will never be weak if self is weak; but when self is strong, faith cannot be strong. For “self” is very much like what gardeners call the “sucker” at the bottom of the tree, which never bears fruit but only draws nourishment away from the tree itself. Self is that sucker which diverts nourishment from faith, and you must cut it out, or your faith will always be “little faith,” and you will find it hard to keep any comfort in your soul.

Christian Gravity

When we profess our faith in Christ, we are not to drape our faces in gloom, but rather to light up our hearts with a purer joy than we ever knew before; and yet we must put away all unfitting silliness. “I said of laughter, it is mad.” I said it, too, on the day my heart was glad. The antics of a madman and the rowdy mirth of a drunkard cannot compare with the calm pleasure of our princely expectations. Walk like people who are looking for the coming of the Son of Man, with this voice in your ears: “What manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness?”

Short-Sightedness

How short-sighted we often are! We think we see the end when we are only looking at the beginning. Sometimes we take out our telescope to look at the future, and we breathe on the lens with the hot breath of our anxiety, and then we think we see clouds and darkness ahead of us. If we are in trouble, we see

“Every day new straits attend, And wonder where the scene will end.”

No, we conclude that it must end in our destruction. We imagine “God hath forgotten to be gracious.” We think “He hath in anger shut up the bowels of compassion.” Oh, this short-sightedness! When you and I ought to believe in God; when we ought to look at the heaven waiting for us and the glory these light afflictions are preparing us for; when we ought to look through the cloud to the eternal sun that never knows an eclipse; when we should be resting on the unseen arm of the immortal God and triumphing in His love, we are mourning and distrusting. May God forgive us for this, and enable us from now on to look not at our troubles but above them, to Him who is guiding us with infinite wisdom and love and has promised to bring us safely through.

Do Not Be Proud, but Fear

While we earnestly seek the full assurance of faith, knowing that it is our strength and our joy, let us also remember that a temptation goes with it. When you have gained this full assurance, believer, get up into your watchtower, because the next temptation will be: “Soul, take it easy; the work is done; you have arrived; now fold your arms and sit still; it will all turn out well; why trouble yourself so much?” Be careful in the times when you have no doubts. “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.” “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” “I said, I shall never be moved. Lord, by Thy favor Thou hast made my mountain to stand strong.” And what comes next? “Thou didst hide Thy face, and I was troubled.” Bless God for full assurance; but remember that nothing but careful living can keep it. Full assurance is a priceless pearl; but when someone carries a precious jewel through the streets, he ought to be very wary of pickpockets. So when the Christian has full assurance, let him be sure that Satan will try to rob him of it. Let him be more careful in how he lives and more diligent in keeping watch than he was before.

A Lesson of Humility

When Jesus sent out His seventy disciples with miraculous powers, they did great wonders, and naturally enough they were rather elated. In their words, “Behold, even devils were subject to us,” Jesus noticed their tendency to pride and self-congratulation. And what sacred lesson did He teach them to keep them from being lifted up too far? “Nevertheless,” He said, “rejoice not in this, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven.” Being sure that we belong to Christ will help keep us humble in times of prosperity. Knowing that we have something better than these earthly blessings acts as a hidden ballast, so that we do not set our affections on earthly things but let our hearts be where our greatest treasure is. Better than any lancet to drain the excess blood of our boasting, better than any bitter medicine to drive away the burning fever of our pride, is this most precious and holy wine of the covenant: remembering that we are safe in Christ. When the Spirit opens this to us, it will be enough to keep us in that happy lowliness that is our true place. But whenever we are cast down by multiplied troubles, the very same fact that kept us humble in prosperity will keep us from despair in adversity. The apostle Paul was surrounded by a great struggle of affliction, and yet he could say, “Nevertheless I am not ashamed.” What kept him from sinking? The same truth that kept the disciples of old from arrogant pride: the sweet conviction that he belonged to Christ. “For I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.” So let us earnestly seek this full assurance of faith, for it will help us in every kind of experience. Let us not rest content until we can say with Paul, “I know whom I have believed.”

fields.title: Providence and the Care of God
fields.body_html:
Tomorrow

If we are not to boast about tomorrows, are they good for nothing? No, blessed be God. There are a great many things we can do with tomorrows. I will tell you what we can do with them if we are God’s children. We can always look forward to them with patience and confidence that they will work together for our good. We can say of our tomorrows, “I do not boast about them, but I am not frightened of them; I would not glory in them, but I will not tremble about them.” Yes, we can be very easy and comfortable about tomorrow. We can remember that all our times are in His hands and all events are at His command; and though we do not know all the twists of the path of providence, He knows them all. They are all settled in His book, and our times are all arranged by His wisdom. So we can look at the tomorrows as we see them in the rough bullion of time, about to be minted into each day’s spending, and say of them all, “They will all be gold; they will all be stamped with the King’s image. So let them come. They will not make me worse; they will work together for my good.”

More than that, a Christian may rightly look forward to his tomorrows not just with resignation but with joy. Tomorrow is a happy thing for a Christian; it is one stage nearer glory. It is one step nearer heaven for a believer, one more knot sailed across the dangerous sea of life, and he is that much nearer his eternal harbour.

Tomorrow! The Christian may rejoice in it. He may say of today, “Day, you may be dark, but I will say goodbye to you, for look, I see tomorrow coming, and I will rise on its wings and fly away, leaving you and your sorrows far behind me.”

All Things working for Good

Christ is the judge of all events. His rule is supreme in everything, and He uses His power for the good of His Church. He spins the thread of events and works from the spindle of destiny, and He does not allow those threads to be woven in any way other than by the pattern of His loving wisdom. He will not let the mysterious wheel turn in any way that does not bring good to His chosen. He makes their worst things blessings to them, and He makes their best things holy. In times of plenty He blesses their increase; in times of famine He supplies all their needs. Just as all things are working for His glory, all things are working for their good.

Unchangeable

There is one place change cannot put its finger on; there is one name on which changeableness can never be written; there is one heart that can never alter. That place is the Most Holy; that heart is God’s; that name is Love.

Providence

The boundless stores of Providence are committed to supporting the believer. Christ is our Joseph, who has granaries full of wheat; but He does not treat us as Joseph treated the Egyptians, for He opens the door of His storehouse and tells us to call everything good in it our own. He has settled on His estate of Providence a permanent charge of a daily portion for us; and He has promised that one day we will see clearly that the estate itself has been well farmed for us and has always been ours. The axle of the wheels of Providence’s chariot is Infinite Love, and Gracious Wisdom is its constant driver.

God’s Tender Care

How careful God is of His people, how concerned He is for them, not only for their lives but for their comfort! Does He say, “Strengthen My people”? Does He say to the angel, “Protect My people”? Does He not say to the heavens, “Drop down manna to feed My people”? His tender care secures all that for them and more. But to show us that He cares not only for our needs but also for our extras, He says, “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people.” He wants us to be not only His living people and His protected people, but His happy people too. He likes His people to be fed; but more than that, He likes to give them “Wines on the lees well refined” to gladden their hearts. He will not only give them “bread”; He will give them “honey” too. He will not just give them “milk”; He will give them “wine and milk.” “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people”: it is the Father’s longing heart, careful even about the little things of His people. “Comfort” that one with tearful eyes; “comfort” that child of Mine with an aching heart; “comfort” that poor grieving one. “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.”

Earth’s Seasons

The things that are seen are pictures of the things that are not seen. The works of creation are pictures, for God’s children, of the hidden mysteries of grace. God’s truths are the apples of gold, and the visible creatures are the baskets of silver. Even the seasons of the year have their parallel in the little world inside a person. We have our winter, dreary, howling winter, when the north wind of the law rushes out against us; when every hope is nipped; when all the seeds of joy lie buried under the dark clods of despair; when our soul is held fast like a river bound with ice, without waves of joy or flowing thanksgiving. Thanks be to God, the soft south wind breathes on our soul, and at once the waters of desire are set free. The spring of love comes on, flowers of hope appear in our hearts, the trees of faith put out their young shoots, the time of the songbirds comes in our hearts, and we have joy and peace in believing through the Lord Jesus Christ. In the believer that happy spring is followed by a rich summer, when his graces are in full bloom like fragrant flowers, loading the air with perfume, and the fruits of the Spirit, like citrons and pomegranates, swell to their full size in the kindly warmth of the Sun of Righteousness. Then comes the believer’s autumn, when his fruits ripen and his fields are ready for harvest. The time has come for his Lord to gather in his “pleasant fruits” and store them in heaven. The feast of ingathering is near: the time when the year will begin again, an unchanging year, like the years of the right hand of the Most High.

God’s Government

There are still people foolish enough to believe that events happen at random, without God’s predestination, and that various disasters take place without the overruling hand or direct action of God. How sad for us, if chance had anything to do with the events of our lives! We would be like poor sailors sent out to sea in an unsafe ship, without a chart and without a rudder. We would know nothing of the harbour we might finally reach. We would only feel that we were now the plaything of the winds, the captives of the storm, and might soon be the victims of the all-devouring deep. We would all be poor orphans if we owed our food and clothing, our present comfort and future prospects, to nothing but chance, with no father’s care to watch over us, left to the fickleness and unreliability of mortal things! What would everything we see around us be but a great sandstorm in the middle of a desert, blinding our eyes and stopping us from ever hoping to see the end through the darkness of the beginning? We would be pilgrims in a pathless wasteland, with no roads to direct us; travellers who might be overturned and overwhelmed at any moment, our bleached bones left as victims of the storm, unknown or forgotten by all. Thank God, it is not like that for us. We believe that everything that happens to us is arranged by the wise and tender will of the One who is our Father and our Friend. We see order in the middle of confusion; we see purposes achieved where others see nothing but emptiness and void. We believe that “He hath His way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet.”

Home-Mercies

When we realize that all our daily mercies come to us as gifts from our Father in heaven, it makes them doubly precious. Nothing tastes as sweet to a schoolboy as what comes from home. It is the same with the Christian. All his mercies are sweeter because they are mercies from home; they come “from above.” The land he lives in is not like the land of Egypt, watered by a river; it “drinketh water of the rain or heaven.” Happy is the person who receives everything like this as coming from God, and thanks his Father for it all! Anything becomes sweet when he knows it comes from heaven. This thought also tends to keep us from an excessive love of the world. The spies went to Eshcol and brought back a huge cluster of the grapes that grew there; but you do not find the people saying, “The fruit we have received from the promised land makes us content to stay in the wilderness.” No; they saw that the grapes came from Canaan, and so they said, “Let us go on and possess the land.” In the same way, when we receive rich mercies, if we thought they came from the natural soil of this earth alone, we might well want to stay here. But if we know they come from a foreign country, we naturally long to go

“Where our dear Lord His vineyard keeps, And all the clusters grow.”

So rejoice, Christian, in the thought that everything you have comes from above. Your daily bread comes not so much from your hard work as from your heavenly Father’s care. You see heaven’s own inscription stamped on every mercy, and every blessing comes down to you perfumed with the ointment, the spikenard and the myrrh of the ivory palaces from which God hands out His gifts.

Changefulness

How varied the believer’s experience is in his spiritual life! What changes there are in the weather of his soul! What bright, sunny days! What dark, cloudy nights! What calms, as if his life were a sea of glass! What terrible trials, as if his life were a stormy ocean! At one time we find him crying, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me,” and soon after he sings, “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me bless His holy name.” One hour we hear him sighing, “I sink in deep mire where there is no standing,” and then we find him exulting, “The Lord is my light, and my salvation, whom shall I fear: the Lord is the strength of my life, of whom shall I be afraid.” How wonderfully he rises to heaven, and how terribly he plunges into the depths! Surely those of us who know anything of the spiritual, inner life are not surprised by this, for we have felt these changes. Sadly, what a contrast there is between the sin that so easily entangles us and the grace that lets us reign in heavenly places. How different is the sorrow of a wretched distrust, which breaks us to pieces like a strong east wind, from the joy of a holy confidence, which carries us on to heaven like a favourable breeze! What changes there are between walking with God today and falling into the mud tomorrow; triumphing over sin, death and hell yesterday and today being led captive by the desires of the flesh and of the mind. Truly, we cannot understand ourselves, and a description that would fit us at one time would fit us badly at another. Our experience is changeable indeed; but oh, what a mercy that Christ does not change! However varied our experience may be, His grace is varied to meet it, for He has grace to help us in every time of need, and with infinite, unfailing goodwill He gives us strength in proportion to our day.

fields.title: Peace and Rest
fields.body_html:
A Quiet Heart

Unless the heart is kept at peace, the life will not be happy. If calm does not reign over the inner lake of the soul that feeds the rivers of our life, the rivers themselves will always be stormy. Our outward actions will always show that they were born in storms by being stormy themselves. We all want to live a joyful life. Bright eyes and a spring in our step are things we all want; carrying a contented mind around is what most people are always aiming for. Let us remember that the only way to keep our life peaceful and happy is to keep the heart at rest. Whether poverty comes or wealth, honour or shame, plenty or scarcity, if the heart is quiet there will be happiness anywhere. But whatever the sunshine and brightness, if the heart is troubled, the whole life must be troubled too.

Peace

At special times the believer enjoys such closeness with the Lord Jesus that his heart is filled with overflowing peace. Oh, there are sweet words Jesus whispers in the ears of His people, and loving visits He pays them, that no one would believe even if he were told. Anyone who wants to understand it must experience in his own heart what it is to have fellowship with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ. Christ really does show Himself to us in a way He does not show Himself to the world. Then all doubting thoughts are driven away, and we can say, “I am my Beloved’s, and my Beloved is mine.” This is the one all-absorbing feeling. And is it any wonder the believer has such deep peace when Christ lives in the heart like this and reigns there without a rival? It would be the miracle of miracles if we did not have peace. But why is our peace not more constant? The only explanation for losing our peace so often is that our communion is broken and our fellowship spoiled; otherwise our peace would be like a river, and our righteousness like the waves of the sea. Live near the cross, and your peace will be continual.

A Place of Trust

Be sure to put all your loved ones into God’s hand. You have put your own soul there; put their souls and bodies into His keeping too. You can trust Him with earthly needs for yourself; trust your jewels to Him. Feel that they are not your own, but God’s loans to you, loans that may be called back at any moment: precious citizens of heaven, not settled on you permanently, but held by you only as a tenant at His will. Your possessions are never so safe as when you are willing to give them up, and you are never so rich as when you put everything you have into the Lord’s hand. You will find that the sorrow of bereavement is greatly eased if, before it comes, you have learned to surrender every day all the things dearest to you into the keeping of your gracious God.

The Savior’s Legacy

“Peace I leave with you.” Here our Saviour means peace with God and peace with our own conscience. Peace with God, for He “hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ,” and now there is “peace on earth” and “good will towards men.” Christ has put our sins away, and so a real, solid peace has been established between God and our souls. This could exist, however, without our clearly understanding it and rejoicing in it. So Christ has given this further witness: peace in the conscience. Peace with God is the treaty; peace with conscience is its announcement. Peace with God is the fountain, and peace with conscience is the crystal stream that flows from it. A peace is decreed in the court of divine justice in heaven; and then, as soon as the news is known, there follows as a necessary result a peace in the lower court of human judgment, where conscience sits on the throne to judge us by our works. So Christ’s legacy is a twofold peace: a peace of friendship, agreement, love and everlasting union between the chosen and God; and a peace of sweet enjoyment, of quiet rest for the understanding and the conscience. When there are no winds above, there will be no storms below; when heaven is calm, earth is quiet. Conscience reflects God’s pleasure. “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

fields.title: Heaven and the Life to Come
fields.body_html:
The Christian’s Crown

Do Christians have a crown? Oh yes, but they do not wear it every day. They have a crown, but their coronation day has not yet come. They have been anointed as kings; they have some of a king’s authority and dignity, only they are not crowned kings yet. But the crown is made. God will not have to order heaven’s goldsmiths to make it later; it is made already, hanging up in glory. God has “laid up for me a crown of righteousness.”

Heaven an Inheritance

“The inheritance of the saints.” So heaven, with all its glories, is an inheritance. Now an inheritance is not something bought with money, earned by work or won by conquest. If anyone has an inheritance in the proper sense of the word, it came to him by birth. And so it is with heaven. The one who receives this glorious inheritance will not get it by the works of the law or by the efforts of the flesh. It will be given to him as a most gracious right, because he has been “begotten again unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,” and so has become an heir of heaven by blood and birth. Those who come to glory are sons; for is it not written, “The Captain of our salvation bringeth many sons unto glory”? They do not come there as servants; no servant has any right to his master’s inheritance. However faithful he is, he is still not his master’s heir. But because you are sons, sons by the Spirit’s new birth and sons by the Father’s adoption, because you have been born again by supernatural power, you become heirs of eternal life and you enter the many rooms of our Father’s house above. So whenever we think of heaven, let us always understand that it is a place that is to be ours, and a state we are to enjoy, as the result of birth, not as the result of work. “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Since that kingdom is an “inheritance,” you can have no claim to enter it until you have the new birth.

The Sleep of Death

“The sleep of death”: what is this sleep? We know that the first idea connected with sleep is rest. The sleeper’s eyes no longer ache from the glare of light or the rush of tears. His ears are no longer pestered by the noise of conflict or the moaning of suffering. His hand is no longer weakened by long, drawn-out effort and painful weariness. His feet are no longer blistered from walking back and forth along a rugged road. There is ease for aching heads, overstrained nerves and heavy hearts in the sweet rest of sleep. On that bed, however hard, the labourer shakes off his toil, the merchant his worry, the thinker his problems and the sufferer his pain. Sleep makes each night a Sabbath for the day. Sleep shuts the door of the soul and tells all intruders to wait a while. So it is with the body as it sleeps in the grave. The weary are at rest; the servant is as much at ease as his master. The worker no longer leans on his spade; the thinker no longer props up his thoughtful head. The wheel stands still; the shuttle no longer moves; the hand that turned the one and the fingers that threw the other are quiet too. The grave shuts out all disturbance, labour and effort. The toil-worn believer sleeps quietly, like a child tired from playing who shuts its eyes and slumbers on its mother’s breast. Oh, happy are those who die in the Lord; they rest from their labours, and their works follow them. We would not avoid work, for though it is a curse in itself, it is a blessing when made holy; yet we would not choose work for work’s sake. And when God’s work is done, we are only too glad to think that our work is done too. When we have finished our day, the mighty Farmer will tell His servants to rest on the best of beds, for the clods of the valley will be sweet to them. Their rest will never be broken until He wakes them to give them their full reward. Guarded by angel watchers, curtained by eternal mysteries, resting in the lap of mother earth, you heirs of glory will sleep on until the fullness of time brings you the fullness of redemption.

Foretastes of Heaven

Can we know anything at all about our heavenly home? Does the human mind have the power to fly into the land of the hereafter where God’s people rest forever? Right at the start our question is met by what seems a flat denial: “Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love Him.” If we stopped there, we might give up all thought of seeing that “goodly land and Lebanon” from here. But we do not stop, for like the apostle we go on with the text and add, “But God hath revealed them unto us by His Spirit.” It is possible to look behind the veil. God’s Spirit can draw it aside for a moment and let us catch a glimpse, even if a distant one, of that indescribable glory. There are “Pisgahs” on earth even now, from whose tops the heavenly Canaan can be seen. There are holy hours when the mists and clouds are swept away and the sun shines in his strength, and our eye, freed from its natural dimness, sees something of that very distant land and a little of the joy and blessedness reserved for God’s people hereafter. Even now, in times of blissful communion, the Holy Spirit gives them experiences, joys and feelings that seem to bring heaven down to them and enable them to grasp, in some faint degree, what heaven itself must be.

Near Home

The best moment of a Christian’s life is the last one, because it is the nearest to heaven; and that is when he begins to strike the keynote of the song he will sing for all eternity. Oh, what a song that will be!

The Way to Heaven

Whatever your hopes may be, there is no way to heaven except through Christ. There is no way to the gates of pearl except through the bleeding side of Jesus. These bleeding wounds are the gates of paradise. If you want to find your way to God’s bright throne, first find your way to Jesus’ cross. If you want to know the way to happiness, walk the path of misery Jesus walked. What! Try another way? Are you mad enough to think you can tear the posts and bars and gates of heaven out of their everlasting places and force your way in by your own created strength? Or do you think you can buy a foothold in paradise with your riches and your gold? Fool!
