What is your gold worth where the streets are made of it and the gates are solid pearl, where the foundations are jasper and the walls are precious gems? And do you think you will get there by your merits? Ah, the angels fell through pride, and through your pride you will fall. Heaven is not for people like you. But do you say, “When I am gone, I will leave my wealth to charities; I will build a hospital or feed the poor”? Then let people pay you. You worked for them; let them pay the debt. Let them put up a stone column and set your statue on top of it. If you have worked for your country, let your country pay you what it owes you. But God, what does He owe you? You have forgotten Him; you have despised His Son; you have rejected His gospel. Be a warrior, a statesman, a patriot, and let people pay you; God owes you nothing. And nothing you can do, if you do not come by the right way, through Jesus Christ, who lived and died and is alive forevermore and has the keys of heaven at His belt, will bribe Him to let you into His palace.

The Hope of Heaven

Believers are not only to be with Christ and see His glory; they are to be like Christ and be glorified with Him. Is He glorious? So will they be. Is He enthroned? So will they be. Does He wear a crown? So will they. Is He a priest? So they will be kings to share His rule, and priests to offer acceptable sacrifices forever. Notice that believers share in everything Christ has. They are to reign with Christ and have a share of His joy, to be honoured with Him and accepted in Him. This is heaven indeed! If you have this hope, I beg you, hold it fast, live on it and rejoice in it.

“A hope so much divine, May trials well endure; May purge your soul from sense and sin, As Christ the Lord is pure.”

Live near your Master now, and your evidences will be bright; and when you come to cross the river, you will see Him face to face, and what that is only those who enjoy it every hour can tell. But if you do not have this bright hope, how can you live content? You are going through a dark world to a darker eternity. I beg you, stop and think. Consider for a moment whether it is worth losing heaven for this poor earth. What! Pawn eternal glories for the pitiful pennies of a few moments of worldly pleasure? No, stop, I beg you; weigh the bargain before you accept it. What will it profit you to gain the whole world and lose your soul? What wailing and gnashing of teeth there will be over the carelessness or mishap by which people lose a heaven like this!

To be with Christ

“To be with Christ.” Who but the Christian can understand this? It is a heaven worldly people do not care about. They do not know what a mass of glory is packed into that one sentence: “To be with Christ.” But to the believer the words are bliss concentrated. Take just one of the many precious thoughts these words suggest: the sight of Christ. “Thine eye shall see the King in His beauty.” We have heard of Him, and we can say, “Whom having not seen we love.” But then we “shall see Him.” Yes, we will actually gaze on the exalted Redeemer. Let the thought sink in. Is there not a heaven in it? You will see the hands that were nailed to the cross for you. You will see the thorn-crowned head, and with all the blood-washed crowd you will bow in humble reverence before Him who bowed in humble lowliness for you. Faith is precious, but what must sight be? To see Jesus as the Lamb of God through the glass of faith makes the soul rejoice with joy beyond words; but oh, to see Him face to face, to look into those eyes, to hear that voice: rapture begins at the very mention of it! If even thinking of it is so sweet, what must the sight be, when we talk with Him “even as a man talketh with his friend”? For seeing Christ implies communion with Him. Everything the bride longed for in Solomon’s Song we will have, and ten thousand times more. Then the prayer will be answered, “Let Him kiss me with the kisses of His mouth: for Thy love is better than wine.” Then we will be able to say, “His left hand is under my head, and His right hand doth embrace me.” Then we will experience the promise, “They shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy.” And then we will pour out the song of gratitude, a song such as we have never sung on earth: tuneful, sweet, pure, full of calm and joy, with no discord to spoil its melody; a rapturous, angelic song. Happy day, when sight and communion will be ours in full, when we will know even as we are known!

fields.title: The Word of God
fields.body_html:
How to Read the Bible

You may read the Bible continuously and still never learn anything from it unless the Spirit lights it up; and then the words shine out like stars. The book seems made of gold leaf, and every single letter glitters like a diamond. Oh, it is a blessed thing to read an illuminated Bible, lit up by the radiance of the Holy Spirit. Have you read the Bible and yet your eyes have not been enlightened? Go and say, “O Lord, light it up; shine on it; for I cannot read it with profit unless You enlighten me.” Blind people may read the Bible with their fingers, but blind souls cannot. We need a light to read the Bible by; there is no reading it in the dark.

The Infallible Commentary

Those who want to know God’s Word best must study it in its own light.

Heart-Learning

We can learn nothing of the gospel except by feeling its truths. Some sciences may be learned with the head, but the science of Christ crucified can only be learned with the heart.

fields.title: Good Works and Diligence
fields.body_html:
Good Works

Once the human heart is put under the microscope of Scripture and we see it with spiritual eyes, we find it so vile that we are quite sure it would be as impossible to expect good works from an unrighteous, unconverted person as to hope to see a fire burning in the middle of the ocean. The two things would not fit together. Our good works, if we have any, spring from a real conversion; and more than that, they spring from a constant spiritual influence at work on us from the time of conversion until the hour of death. Christian, you would have no good works if you did not have fresh grace day by day! You would not find that the grace given you in the first hour was enough to produce fruit today. It is not like a tree planted in our hearts that naturally bears fruit by itself; the sap rises from the root, Jesus Christ. We are not trees on our own; we are branches attached to the Living Vine.

Our good works spring from union with Christ. The more someone knows and feels that he is one with Jesus, the holier he will be. Why is a Christian’s character like Christ’s character? For this reason only: he is joined and united to the Lord Jesus. Why does the branch produce grapes? Simply because it has been grafted into the vine and so shares the nature of the stem. So, Christian, the only way you can bear fruit for God is by being grafted into Christ and united with Him. If you think you can walk in holiness without keeping up constant fellowship with Christ, you have made a great mistake. If you want to be holy, you must live close to Jesus. Good works spring only from there. This gives us the strongest reasons against anything like trusting in works. For since works are only God’s gift, how utterly impossible it is for an unconverted person to produce any such good works in himself. And if they are God’s gifts, how little of our own merit can there be in them!

Begin Well

I have known people run the race of faith with all their might and still lose it because they did not start right. You say, “Well, how does that happen?” There are some people who suddenly leap into religion. They get it quickly, keep it for a while, and in the end lose it because they did not get their religion the right way. They have heard that before someone can be saved, he needs, by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, to feel the weight of sin, to confess it, to give up all hope in his own works and to look to Jesus Christ alone. They regard all these things as unpleasant preliminaries; and so, before they have attended to repentance, before the Holy Spirit has done a good work in them, before they have been brought to give up everything and trust in Christ, they make a profession of faith. This is like setting up in business without any stock, and it is bound to fail. If someone has no capital to start with, he may put on a fine show for a little while, but it will be like the crackling of thorns under a pot: a lot of noise and plenty of light for a short time, but it will die out in darkness. How many there are who never think there needs to be any work in the heart! Let us remember, though, that no one has ever had a changed heart without first having a miserable heart. We must pass through that black tunnel of conviction before we can come out onto the high embankment of holy joy; we must first go through the Slough of Despond before we can run along the Walls of Salvation. There must be ploughing before there is sowing; there must be many frosts and many sharp showers before there is any reaping. But we often act like little children who pick flowers from the bushes and plant them in their gardens without roots, and then say how beautiful and pretty their little garden is. But wait a while, and all their flowers have withered, because they have no roots. That is the result of not starting right, of not having “the root of the matter.” What good is outward religion, its flowers and leaves, unless we have “the root of the matter” in us, unless we have been ploughed with the plough of the Spirit and then sown with the sacred seed of the Gospel, in hope of bringing forth a plentiful harvest? There must be a good start in running the Christian race, because there is no hope of winning unless the start is right.

Freely Give

Christian, whenever you are tempted to hold back from God’s Church out of greed, think of your Saviour giving up everything He had to serve you! When you see self-denial as noble as that, can you then be selfish, and count your luxuries more important than the needs of the poor of the flock when their claims are pressed on you? Remember Jesus. Imagine you see Him looking at you and saying, “I gave Myself for you, and do you hold yourself back from Me? If you do, you do not know My love in all its heights and depths and lengths and breadths.”

Obedience to God’s Will

For the Christian, no argument is as powerful as God’s will. God’s will is the believer’s law. He does not ask what profit it will bring him or what good effect it will have on others; he simply asks, “Does my Father command it?” And his prayer is, “O Holy Spirit, help me to obey, not because I see how it will be good for me, but simply because You command it.” It is the Christian’s privilege to do God’s commandments, “Hearkening to the voice of His Word.”

The Glad Command

“Delight thyself in the Lord.” This one-command law is no stony law to be carved on slabs of granite. It contains a command so sparklingly bright that it deserves to be written on amethysts and pearls. “Delight thyself in the Lord.” When delight becomes a duty, duty must surely be a delight. When it becomes my duty to be happy, and I have an explicit command to be glad, I must be foolish indeed if I refuse my own joys and turn away from my own happiness. Oh, what a God we have, who has made it our duty to be happy! What a gracious God, who counts no obedience as worthy of His acceptance as glad obedience offered by a joyful heart. “Delight thyself in the Lord.”

Idleness

Some temptations come to the hard-working, but all temptations attack the idle. Idle Christians are not so much tempted by the devil as they tempt the devil to tempt them. Idleness leaves the door of the heart open and invites Satan in. But if we are busy from morning till night and Satan gets in, he will have to break the door down. Under sovereign grace, and next to faith, there is no better shield against temptation than obeying the command to be “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.”

Usefulness

Christ, my Master, went about doing good, and if you want to walk with Him, you must go about on the same mission.

Faith Shown in Life

I would not give much for your religion unless it can be seen. Lamps do not talk, but they do shine. A lighthouse beats no drum and sounds no gong, and yet its friendly spark is visible to the sailor far across the water. So let your actions shine out your faith. Let all your conduct illustrate the main sermon of your life, and it cannot fail to be illustrious.

Christian Diligence

We find in Scripture that most of the great appearances to outstanding saints came while they were busy. Moses was keeping his father-in-law’s flock when he saw the burning bush. Joshua was going around the city of Jericho when he met the angel of the Lord. Jacob was praying when the angel of God appeared to him. Gideon was threshing and Elisha was ploughing when the Lord called them. Matthew was at the tax booth when he was told to follow Jesus, and James and John were fishing. The Almighty Lover of human souls does not usually show Himself to idle people. Whoever is lazy and inactive cannot expect to have the sweet company of his Saviour.

fields.title: The Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
Divine Teaching

In the depths of trouble we learn how sufficient grace is. Well may they “glory in tribulations also” who have learned the most profitable lessons of grace in them, proved in them how ample the supply of grace is, and found in them that the triumph of grace is certain. I do not know whether all soldiers love the thought of war. Some do; many long for a campaign. How often a junior officer has grumbled, “There is no promotion, no hope of rising, no honours, no prize money, as there would be if we had to fight. If we could charge the cannon’s mouth, there would be some prospect of being promoted.” People who never smell gunpowder get few medals to pin on their chests. The brave days, as people call them, of Nelson and Trafalgar are gone, and we thank God for it. Still, we do not expect to see veterans of this age as brave as the old ones still found in our hospitals, survivors of our old campaigns. No, brothers and sisters, we must have trials if we are to make progress. Young men do not become midshipmen just by going to the school at Greenwich and climbing the mast on dry land; they must go to sea. We must do business in great waters; we must actually be on deck in a storm if we want to see the works of the Lord and His wonders in the deep. We must have stood side by side with King David; we must have gone down into the pit to kill the lion, or lifted the spear against the eight hundred, if we want to know the saving strength of God’s right hand. Conflicts bring experience, and experience brings a growth in grace that cannot be reached any other way.

The Work of the Spirit

Let us always remember that Christ on the cross is of no value to us without the Holy Spirit in us. The blood flows in vain unless the Spirit’s finger applies it to our conscience. The garment of righteousness was made in vain unless the Holy Spirit wraps it around us and clothes us in its costly folds. The river of the water of life cannot quench our thirst until the Spirit offers the cup and lifts it to our lips. Nothing in the paradise of God could ever bring us bliss as long as we are dead souls; and dead we are, until that heavenly wind comes and breathes on us so that we may live. We do not hesitate to say that we owe as much to God the Holy Spirit as we do to God the Son. Indeed, it would be a grave sin and offence to try to put one person of the divine Trinity before another. You, O Father, are the source of all grace, all love and mercy toward us. You, O Son, are the channel of Your Father’s mercy, and without You Your Father’s love could never flow to us. And You, O Spirit, are the One who enables us to receive the divine power that flows from the fountainhead, the Father, through Christ the channel, and that by Your work enters our heart, stays there and brings forth its glorious fruit. So magnify the Spirit. There has never yet been a heavenly thought, a holy deed or a consecrated act acceptable to God through Jesus Christ that was not worked in us by the Holy Spirit.

fields.title: The Church and the World
fields.body_html:
The One Family

God’s universe is one. Heaven and earth are not as separate as unbelief has imagined. Just as the Lord has only one family, written in one register, redeemed with one blood and brought to life by one Spirit, so this whole household lives in one home forever. We who are in the body live in the lower room. It is sometimes dark and cold, but it bears enough marks to show that it is a room in God’s house; for to the eye of faith it is often lit with heavenly brightness, and even we, while still here, are made sharers in the inheritance of the saints in light through blessed foretastes. It is the same house, I say, but ours is the lower room, while our glorified brothers and sisters are up in the upper floor, where the sunlight streams in forever and no chilling winds or poisonous breath can ever reach. And to a large extent the lower room resembles the upper room. Just as on earth we prepare for heaven, the state of the saints on earth is heaven foreshadowed. In many ways the condition of God’s child on earth is a picture of his condition in heaven; and whatever the character of the saints above is, that should be the character of the saints below. We may very safely take those glorified spirits as our example. We need not fear being led astray by imitating them, learning their occupations or trying to share their joys. Surely the things in heaven are patterns for the things on earth, and as they are before the throne, so we ought to be. More than that, so we will be, to the extent that we live up to our privileges and receive the likeness and image of our Lord Jesus Christ.

A Few Names Even in Sardis

“Thou hast a few names even in Sardis, which have not defiled their garments.” Here we have special preservation. Note it carefully. “Thou hast a few names.” Only a few; not as few as some think, but not as many as others imagine. A few compared with the mass of those who profess faith; a few compared even with God’s true children, for many of them have soiled their garments. There were only a few, and those few were even in Sardis. There is no Church on earth so corrupt that it does not have “a few.”

Take heart, Christians; there are a few in Sardis. Do not be completely downcast. Some heroes have not turned their backs on the day of battle; some mighty men still fight for the truth. But be careful, for perhaps you are not one of the “few.” Since there are only “a few,” there ought to be great searching of hearts. Let us look at our garments and see whether they are soiled. And since there are only “a few,” be active. The fewer workers there are to do the work, the more reason you have to be active. “Be instant in season, out of season.” Oh, if we had hundreds behind us, we might say, “Let them do the work;” but if we stand with only “a few,” how hard each of those few should work!

So stir yourselves up to the greatest activity, for truly there are only a few in Sardis who have not soiled their garments. Above all, be prayerful. Send up your earnest cries to God that He would multiply the faithful, increase the number of chosen ones who stand firm, and purify the Church. Cry to God for the day to come when the fine gold will no longer be dim, when the glory will return to Zion again. Beg God to remove the cloud and take away “the darkness that may be felt.” Be doubly prayerful, for there are only a few in Sardis who have not soiled their garments.

The Church and the World

Christians ought to live in such a way that it would be pointless to speak of a comparison between them and the people of the world. It should not be a comparison but a contrast. No sliding scale should be possible; the believer should be a direct and obvious contradiction of the unregenerate. The life of a saint should be entirely above, and in a different class from, the life of a sinner. We should force our critics not to admit that moralists are good and Christians a little better. Rather, while the world is darkness, we should plainly be light; and while the world lies in the power of the Wicked One, we should very evidently belong to God and overcome the Wicked One’s temptations. Life and death, light and darkness, purity and sin are as far apart as the poles. There should be as much difference between the worldly person and the Christian as between hell and heaven, between destruction and eternal life. Just as we hope that in the end a great gulf will separate us from the fate of the unrepentant, there should be a deep, wide gulf here between us and the ungodly. Our character should be so pure that people must take note of us as being of another, higher race. If we were what we claim to be, there would be no difficulty in telling the Christian from the worldly person. But sadly the Church is so watered down that we have to tone down our boasting and cannot exalt our character as we would like. Oh, for the time when “our conversation shall be in heaven,” and the worldly person’s base life will be rebuked by our Christlike character! May God grant that more and more we may be plainly a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for His own possession, so that we may show forth the praises of Him who called us out of darkness into His marvellous light.
